items.title: RAF launches first ever space squadron dedicated to defending Britain's satellites
items.summary: The RAF has launched No. III Space Effects Squadron, its first dedicated unit to counter hostile threats to UK satellites.
items.body:
New No. III Space Effects Squadron will be the UK’s first unit dedicated to disrupting, degrade, and deny hostile threats in space.

The squadron will protect the critical satellites that guide British ships, connect mobile phones and warn of missile attacks.

Forms a key part of the UK’s ability to gain and maintain freedom to operate in space, as set out in the government’s Space Strategy published this month.

Satellites vital to everyday life in the UK are set to be protected from hostile threats, as the RAF launches the UK’s first ever dedicated space squadron focused on disrupting, degrading, and denying enemy activity targeting British interests in space.

Announced today by the Chief of the Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smith at the first-ever UK Space Power Conference, No. III Space Effects Squadron will bring together specialist personnel from across the Armed Forces to counter hostile activity in orbit and defend the satellites the nation depends on every day.

While sister units No. I Space Operations Squadron and No. II Space Warning Squadron give the RAF the ability to watch and warn of threats in space, the new No. III Squadron will act against those threats, using advanced technology, including Electronic Warfare, to disrupt, degrade and deny hostile actions. The squadron will support both offensive and defensive space operations and will expand over time as new capabilities enter service.

It comes as the Defence Secretary Wes Streeting will give a keynote address at the Space Conference.

He is expected to say:

Britain has to keep pace in the new space race. Control of the waves was the essential ingredient in 19th century deterrence. That is why Britain built the finest naval power in history. In the 20th century it was control of the skies, and so we built a world class air force to protect us. This century will depend on control of space. Our dependency on space is precisely why it is increasingly under threat from our adversaries. That threat is growing in scale, speed, and sophistication. And challenges in space increasingly mirror the geopolitics on Earth. My job is to make sure that our deterrence in space is as strong as it is on Earth, and to modernise our armed forces so that they are ready to deter and, if necessary, defeat any adversary, in any domain.

In the 20th century it was control of the skies, and so we built a world class air force to protect us. This century will depend on control of space.

Our dependency on space is precisely why it is increasingly under threat from our adversaries. That threat is growing in scale, speed, and sophistication. And challenges in space increasingly mirror the geopolitics on Earth.

My job is to make sure that our deterrence in space is as strong as it is on Earth, and to modernise our armed forces so that they are ready to deter and, if necessary, defeat any adversary, in any domain.

Satellites are a core part of national security and support daily life across the UK. They are critical to intelligence gathering and missile warning, but also power mobile phone data, weather forecasts and online ordering. Ambulances, firefighters and the police rely on satellite navigation systems for emergency responses, and energy networks use the same systems to organise power grids.

As space becomes more crowded and more dangerous – with hostile states developing capabilities to jam, disrupt or disable space assets – the government is taking action to defend UK interests in space, while maintaining an operational advantage for our armed forces.

The Chief of the Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, said:

Space no longer supports operations from the sidelines. It’s a domain of direct competition, where our military advantage can be won or lost. No. III Space Effects Squadron will safeguard the vital benefits that space gives to our integrated armed forces, and will be capable of denying those benefits to our adversaries.

Space no longer supports operations from the sidelines. It’s a domain of direct competition, where our military advantage can be won or lost.

No. III Space Effects Squadron will safeguard the vital benefits that space gives to our integrated armed forces, and will be capable of denying those benefits to our adversaries.

The formation of No. III Space Effects Squadron contributes to the UK’s developing capabilities for space warfare, including Electronic Warfare and countermeasures against anti-satellite weapons.

The work delivers on the UK’s Control of Space Requirement - the need to maintain freedom to operate in space, and deny adversaries the same freedom. The Requirement was set out in the UK Space Strategy published earlier this month, and builds on the Strategic Defence Review, which made clear that the ability to operate in, from and through space underpins the UK’s security, prosperity and daily way of life.

While taking action to protect critical space infrastructure, the government remains committed to the peaceful and sustainable use of space.

The UK has formally ruled out destructive anti-satellite missile testing and continues to work through the UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space to promote norms, rules and principles of responsible space behaviours.

That commitment underpins the UK’s continuous work with allies and partners to strengthen collective defence in space, including an £880 million investment between 2026/27 and 2029/30 in space-based Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance and space control activities.

items.title: Okinawa chiefs don covers, receive anchors
items.author: PO2 Zachary Guth
items.summary: Okinawa welcomed its newest members to the rank of chief petty officer at Keystone Theater on Kadena Air Base on Sept. 16, 2026. Nineteen Sailors were pinned to chief petty officer alongside five U.S. Marines and one U.S. Air Force Airman as honorary chief petty officers.
items.body:
KADENA AIR BASE, Japan – Okinawa welcomed its newest members to the rank of chief petty officer at Keystone Theater on Kadena Air Base on Sept. 16, 2026. Nineteen Sailors were pinned to chief petty officer alongside five U.S. Marines and one U.S. Air Force Airman as honorary chief petty officers.

The chief pinning ceremony represents the culminations of six weeks of physical, mental and emotional training. Families and mentors were welcomed on stage to pin the fouled anchor onto the new chiefs and don them with the chief petty officer cover. For the first time in their career, they bear the uniform of a chief petty officer.

“Six weeks did not magically turn you into a chief. A chief is built, with time, with mistakes, long nights, hard lessons, difficult conversations, and repeated reminders that the job is bigger than your ego,” said Command Master Chief Frank Queenlacombe, Naval Mobile Construction Battalion 5 senior enlisted leader, during his remarks. “Today is not the finish line. It is your second beginning, your second birthday.”

Two of the 19 Sailors selected for promotion to chief petty officer on Okinawa belong to Commander, Fleet Activities Okinawa’s security department.

“I am incredibly grateful to reach this milestone at CFAO, surrounded by fellow chiefs and officers who have made a lasting impact on my career and the Sailor I have become,” said Chief Master-at-Arms Brandon Hodges. “I wouldn’t be here without the people who have believed in me, pushed me to grow and supported me throughout this journey. Their guidance and support have meant more to me than I can put into words.”

In total the chief pinning ceremony brought together six naval commands across the island of Okinawa, along with the five Marine commands and one Air Force command. Together, they forged their leadership, their ideals, communicated with their mentorship and laid the groundwork for a new chapter in their lives.

“You don’t change who you are because you become a chief, it only enhances you,” said newly pinned Chief Sonar Technician (Submarines) Tony Holman, assigned to Navy Data Center Detachment Okinawa. “You go from being a leader by yourself, to understanding that you can’t do it alone. That you’re not a chief to just your Sailors but to everybody.”

The Navy rank of chief petty officer holds special regard amongst the U.S Armed Forces, a tradition going back 133 years, with those selected moving into roles of great responsibility and leadership. With the striking of two bells and the whistle of the boatswain’s pipe, the chiefs carry the weight of the anchor as they salute the side boys for the first time.

“The chief petty officer pinning is a public display of an outward, visible dedication—an acceptance of the responsibility to provide servant leadership to the sons and daughters whom we are entrusted to lead into harm’s way every day,’ said Command Master Chief Aaron Belcher, Commander, Fleet Activities Okinawa senior enlisted leader, after the pinning ceremony. “We achieved this through the support of everyone along our journey and the relentless hard work of our Sailors.”

He concluded, “Ultimately, the pinning ceremony provides total transparency into the expectations of a chief, serving as a public dedication to being present, meaningful leaders on the deck plates."

items.title: MAG-24 Marines train with Army, Air Force to rapidly repair damaged airfields
items.author: Sgt Anabelle Reedobrien
items.summary: MARINE CORPS TRAINING AREA BELLOWS, Hawaii — Sept. 14-17, 2026, service members from Marine Wing Support Squadron 174, Marine Aircraft Group 24 trained with the Army’s 130th Engineer Brigade and the Air Force’s 647th Civil Engineer Squadron to sharpen the joint force's ability to rapidly repair damaged airfields. This joint training strengthened interoperability and readiness, enhancing the U.S. military's ability to operate in austere environments.
items.body:
MARINE CORPS TRAINING AREA BELLOWS, Hawaii — Sept. 14-17, 2026, service members from Marine Wing Support Squadron 174, Marine Aircraft Group 24 trained with the Army’s 130th Engineer Brigade and the Air Force’s 647th Civil Engineer Squadron to sharpen the joint force's ability to rapidly repair damaged airfields. This joint training strengthened interoperability and readiness, enhancing the U.S. military's ability to operate in austere environments.

Runways are critical to aviation operations in any environment. During a crisis, the speed that repair crews respond can determine how quickly flight operations resume. This joint airfield damage repair (JADR) exercise involved a realistic scenario with service members assessing and repairing large craters simulating the kind of damage that may be encountered in contested environments. After assessing and clearing out the damaged areas, service members used a special form of rapid-setting cement to repair the simulated craters.

“This training impacts the Marine Corps in a lot of ways,” said 2nd Lt. Zachary Kolb, JADR officer in charge, with MWSS-174. “Working with partnered forces prepares us for future operations while giving the Marines a realistic exercise that covers all aspects of airfield damage repair.”

While technical proficiency was a key focus, the broader value was in standardizing the process across military branches and preparing participants for future operations. Participating units coordinated their efforts through a shared command post, emphasizing teamwork alongside technical proficiency. The joint structure enabled the services to align planning, streamline communications and synchronize their distinct technical procedures.

“It’s always a great experience working with different branches,” said Lance Cpl. Mark Rummel, a combat engineer, with MWSS-174. “It's eye-opening to learn how they operate and their unique strategy for getting the mission done.”

As the dust settled over Marine Corps Training Area Bellows, Marines, soldiers and Airmen packed their gear with a clearer understanding of how their specialized capabilities support the joint force. By working together to solve complex logistical challenges, they refined a standardized approach to repairing damaged airfields giving commanders more reliable options to rapidly restore flight operations and project airpower from remote locations in contested environments.

items.title: From enlisted infantryman to scout platoon leader: 1st Lt. Nalepa's path through the Army
items.author: MAJ Ian Roth
items.summary: AULI, India — Before 1st Lt. Maximilian Nalepa led a scout platoon through the Himalayas during Exercise Yudh Abhyas 2026, he spent four years as an enlisted infantryman, a path he chose deliberately before ever putting on officer's rank.
items.body: AULI, India — Before 1st Lt. Maximilian Nalepa led a scout platoon through the Himalayas during Exercise Yudh Abhyas 2026, he spent four years as an enlisted infantryman, a path he chose deliberately before ever putting on officer's rank. Nalepa, the scout platoon leader for 1st Battalion, 5th Infantry Regiment, 1st Mobile Brigade Combat Team, 11th Airborne Division, grew up in a suburb of Chicago and enlisted in the Army in 2016. He served four years as an infantryman before attending West Point through the Army's enlisted-to-commissioning program, commissioning as an officer in 2024. "There were a lot of things that I wanted to do and accomplish, and challenges that I wanted to face, that I felt would be better to face as a soldier," Nalepa said. "I wanted to serve in the Ranger Regiment, and was fortunate enough to do so. I wanted to go to Ranger School. I wanted to deploy. Those things created a lot of meaning for me, and a lot of lessons that I've been able to take with me and help share with my soldiers." Nalepa said his enlisted time shapes how he leads his platoon today, most of whom are under the age of 25. He said understanding what his soldiers are working toward in their own careers, and reducing the obstacles in their way, has become a priority for him and his platoon sergeant. "We've been able to build a culture around advancing their careers, around helping Soldiers reach the goals, whatever they may be for that individual," Nalepa said. "For some, that's not their plan. There are guys who plan on getting out, but we invest a lot of time in making sure they have the resources and the knowledge of what they should be doing to progress, and setting them up with people or organizations that'll help them along the way." That investment has produced results. Nalepa said four soldiers in the platoon recently earned slots to Ranger School, and four or five more are at various stages of packets for Special Forces Assessment and Selection. He and his platoon sergeant served as the battalion's officer in charge and noncommissioned officer in charge for its pre-Ranger program. For Nalepa's platoon, YA26 has meant working through subject matter expert exchanges with the Indian Army's sniper and drone units, building on an exchange the platoon conducted in April at the Indian Army Sniper School in Mhow, India. Nalepa said the experience has given many of his soldiers their first look at how a non-Western military operates. "There's an immense benefit to working with a partner force that is not a Western military," Nalepa said. "I've worked with other Western armies previously, and there's a lot of carryover, a lot of similarity. Here, with the largest country by population in the world, learning how to form partnerships with this is an incredible asset that will enable many of my subordinate leaders, and then soldiers, to be successful in other joint trainings throughout the Pacific." Nalepa pointed to differences in command structure as one example. He said Indian Army noncommissioned officers operate under a more rigid chain of command with less mission command authority than their U.S. counterparts, a contrast that has given his own junior NCOs a clearer appreciation for the autonomy built into how the U.S. Army operates. Nalepa said he wants his soldiers to leave YA26 with both the technical skills gained from training alongside the Indian Army and an appreciation for the opportunity itself. He pointed to soldiers repelling down a cliff face, firing foreign weapons systems and preparing to visit a temple in the region with a history spanning thousands of years, experiences many of them would not otherwise have. "Every leader, whether it's a senior specialist who's leading his peers, a team leader, a squad leader, all the way up the chain of command, is making a difference on their subordinates and significantly affecting the direction those individuals will go," Nalepa said. "Being around junior soldiers, being able to help set conditions for them to have successful careers and find meaning and purpose for themselves, is where myself and my platoon sergeant get a lot of value in what we do." Nalepa said he plans to attend Special Forces Assessment and Selection before reaching his maneuver captain's career course date, roughly 18 months away. Since 2004, Yudh Abhyas, a U.S. Army Pacific-sponsored bilateral exercise with the Indian Army, has enhanced combined interoperability and strengthened the U.S.-India Major Defense Partnership in support of a free and open Indo-Pacific.

items.title: Ritsumeikan University students have lunch with CLR 37 Commanding Officer
items.author: Cpl Anakin Smith
items.summary: U.S. Marine Corps Col. Robert Gerbracht, commanding officer of Combat Logistics Regiment 37, 3rd Marine Logistics Group, hosted approximately 20 students from Ritsumeikan University in Kyoto, Japan, for lunch at the Mess Hall on Camp Kinser, Okinawa, Japan, Sept. 15, 2026.
items.body:
CAMP KINSER, Okinawa, Japan — U.S. Marine Corps Col. Robert Gerbracht, commanding officer of Combat Logistics Regiment 37, 3rd Marine Logistics Group, hosted approximately 20 students from Ritsumeikan University in Kyoto, Japan, for lunch at the Mess Hall on Camp Kinser, Okinawa, Japan, Sept. 15, 2026.

The visit allowed students to experience life aboard a military installation, have a better understanding of the purpose and mission of the U.S. military in Japan, and be able to interact with Marines. The visit was personally significant to Gerbracht, who attended Ritsumeikan University from 2009 to 2011.

“It was great to see them, not only as student from the same university but as people”, said Gerbracht. “We’re able to interact with a whole new generation of students that are there and get to share an experience with them.”

Gerbracht and his wife were both selected for the Olmstead Scholar Program, a military education program that awards scholarships to highly qualified, active-duty junior officers in the United States military in order to pursue language studies and overseas graduate-level education. The scholar program provides one year of foreign language training followed by two years of study at a foreign graduate school.

“My wife and I both applied in 2008”, said Gerbracht. “We actually ended up being the first married couple to be selected for the Olmsted program.”

Students with Ritsumeikan University traveled from mainland Japan to Okinawa as part of a university culture trip to the island, and it is frequent that this trip includes a visit to Camp Kinser. The students got to sit down with Marines while aboard the base, allowing them to learn more about each other's ways of life.

“I spoke with some of the students about the differences between Japanese culture and American culture.” said Gerbracht. “But there's also a lot of similarities between what we value as Marines and what a lot of Japanese people value.”

During his time at Ritsumeikan University Gerbracht earned his master's degree in international relations. Learning the language and experiencing the culture has helped Gerbracht in his current position as commanding officer a forward-deployed logistics regiment as well as base commander of the Urasoe-based Camp Kinser, in addition to paying dividends at his other duty stations as well.

“The way you lead better is by having a broad base of knowledge.” said Gerbracht, “It’s like having 1,000 keys to locks you haven’t seen yet.”

items.title: 18th TMC leads Army forces during Trident Resolve 26 in Indonesia
items.author: 1LT Maddy Gonzalez and SFC Timothy Hughes
items.summary: U.S. Army Pacific’s 18th Theater Medical Command is serving as the Army Forces Headquarters for Exercise Trident Resolve 2026 in Banten Province, Indonesia, Sept. 20–26. Co-hosted by the United States and Indonesia, the exercise brings together ASEAN and ADMM-Plus partners to strengthen cooperation across military medicine, cybersecurity, and humanitarian assistance and disaster relief. Participants will conduct a simulated multinational response to an earthquake and tsunami while supporting loc
items.body:
BANTEN, Indonesia – Personnel from the U.S. Army Pacific 18th Theater Medical Command (TMC) arrived in Banten Province on the island of Java to serve as the Army Forces Headquarters (ARFOR HQ) for Exercise Trident Resolve 2026, Sept. 20-26.

Co-hosted by the United States and Indonesia, XTR 26 is the first field training exercise under the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Defense Ministers Meeting- Plus (ADMM-Plus) framework to integrate three Experts’ Working Groups: Military Medicine, Cybersecurity, and Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR).

"Trident Resolve 2026 is a tremendous opportunity for us to advance vital health security cooperation and enhance joint interoperability," said U.S. Army Maj. Gen. E. Darrin Cox, commanding general of the 18th TMC and co-chair of the Military Medicine Experts’ Working Group. “Over the next week, the 18th TMC, alongside our Army augmentees and sister services, will strengthen critical bonds with ASEAN partners, ensuring our collective medical, cyber and disaster response forces are prepared to prevail in the face of regional crises.”

As the lead unit for USARPAC during the exercise, the 18th TMC is responsible for the command, control and coordination of all participating U.S. Army forces and individual augmentees. The ARFOR HQ is also supported by key regional enablers, including I Corps, the 62nd Medical Brigade and the 8th Theater Sustainment Command.

During the exercise, TR26 participants will simulate a multinational response to an earthquake and tsunami in western Indonesia. Concurrently, joint and combined forces will deliver real-world infrastructure and community health projects, including public health screenings, facility renovations and infectious disease subject matter exchanges that will directly benefit local communities.

Participating nations include the 11 ASEAN member states and key ADMM-Plus dialogue partners, including Australia, India, Japan, New Zealand, the Republic of Korea, among others.

Through multinational cooperation and innovation, Trident Resolve 2026 reinforces the enduring U.S. commitment to ASEAN centrality and a free, open and resilient Pacific. The exercise exemplifies USARPAC’s focus on investing in people, strengthening partnerships, prevailing in crisis, and driving continuous transformation across the region.

U.S. participants include service members assigned to the U.S. Army, U.S. Air Force, and Hawaii National Guard supporting its Hawii State Partnership Program: United States Pacific Command (PACOM), 51st Medical Group, 374th Medical Group, Pacific Air Forces, 62nd Medical Brigade, Navy Environmental and Preventative Medicine Unit Six, 130th Engineer Brigade, 8th Theater Sustainment Command, Hawaii Medical Readiness Detachment, and 298th Multi-Functional Training Regiment.

items.title: U.S. Army Japan Ten-Miler team doesn’t let geographical separation prevent them from training together
items.author: Noriko Kudo
items.summary: CAMP ZAMA, Japan – “Running might seem like an individual effort, but you perform better as a team,” Spc. Stephanie Feliciano Vazquez said.
items.body: CAMP ZAMA, Japan – “Running might seem like an individual effort, but you perform better as a team,” Spc. Stephanie Feliciano Vazquez said. That philosophy is driving Feliciano Vazquez, assigned to the 38th Air Defense Artillery Brigade, and other members of the U.S. Army Japan Army Ten-Miler team as they prepare for the upcoming race Oct. 11 in Washington, D.C., transforming weekly team practices into a showcase of collective strength. For Spc. Junho Yi, assigned to the 311th Military Intelligence Battalion, that team dynamic provides an essential spark during demanding training — even across great distances throughout Japan. Using live video feeds during practice, the Camp Zama squad trains side-by-side with remote teammates Capt. David Ford and Staff Sgt. Ryan Figgins, also assigned to 38th ADA, at Okinawa and the Shariki Communications Site; and Sgt. Xaviar Estrada, assigned to the 765th Transportation (Terminal) Battalion at Yokohama North Dock. “I usually run alone, so I lose motivation,” Yi said. “Running with teammates gives me that extra push. It’s always better to run with somebody. We try to run together and pace off each other.” That virtual and in-person connection translates directly to higher performance targets. Rather than simply participating, the squad said it helps them set aggressive personal and team benchmarks together. “Our team goal isn’t just to be there — it’s to go out and compete,” Yi said. “My personal goal is running 10 miles in under one hour.” Feliciano Vazquez echoed the drive to build lasting momentum. “Every time we meet, we push each other to get better and make the team and each other proud,” she said. “We want to keep this Army Ten-Miler team going every single year from now on, building a legacy that continues next year and beyond.”

items.title: The KC-130J: Past, present and the future fight
items.author: CPT Rebekah Harasick
items.summary: Operation Slingshot demonstrated the KC-130J's current ability to enable critical power projection for the Marine Corps, using its heavy payload capacity to leapfrog ahead of F-35B fighter jets. The KC-130J lands at remote, undeveloped airfields to establish Aviation-Delivered Ground Refueling and re-arming points. During this self-supported movement, the KC-130J traversed a route from Royal Australian Air Force Base Tindal, Australia, through Cairns, Pohnpei, the Kwajalein Atoll, and Wake Islan
items.body:
In the vast, unpredictable Indo-Pacific, islands dot the expanse of the sea for miles. Close enough to be a positive, yet far enough apart and sparsely populated to qualify as austere. This part of the world doesn't provide an answer to accessibility, and that question gets even foggier when you employ strategy and tactics.

But 3d Marine Aircraft Wing (MAW) has an answer: the KC-130J, an aviation platform built for this exact venture. Operation Slingshot is a proof-of-concept strategy hailing from historic times when the Corps used island-hopping to win wars, and although aviation platforms are sleeker and more technologically advanced today, the need for Marines across the globe has not changed. The KC-130J's ability to extend reach gives pilots the ability to strike fast and move faster as they conduct "the slingshot." In this part of the world, it is not just an advantage; it is a necessity.

For the 3d MAW KC-130J, projecting power across thousands of miles of ocean requires more than the fighter jets you see in Top Gun. It requires a lifeline.

During Operation Slingshot, the KC-130J successfully projected 3d MAW, along with F-35B Lightning II fighters, across 4,000 nautical miles of the Indo-Pacific, into locations secured by Marines using MV-22B Ospreys and other components of the wing.

Drawing on a legacy established during the siege of Khe Sanh and Operation Desert Storm, the KC-130J operated as a self-contained logistical node, establishing forward refueling points without reliance on external strategic tankers.

Since its introduction, the C-130 platform has served the United States military and the Marine Corps as the logistical backbone of aviation. Originally birthed out of necessity during the Korean War, its inception after the maiden flight in Marietta, out of the Lockheed-Georgia Company facility in 1955, marked the start of a new era. During the 1968 siege of Khe Sanh in Vietnam, C-130s lived up to their designed intent, delivering over 12,000 tons of supplies via paradrops and austere landings and keeping the surrounded 26th Marines supplied when overland routes were severed. Decades later, during Operation Desert Storm in 1991, Marine KC-130s continued to demonstrate that same prowess with extended capabilities, providing the critical aerial refueling necessary to project strike packages deep into the northern Persian Gulf. The KC-130J solidified its position in aviation through enhanced multi-mission functionality, all while retaining the transport versatility of its roots.

Today, the Indo-Pacific theater demands the same endurance and adaptability, updated for the modern battlefield. Operation Slingshot demonstrated the KC-130J's current ability to enable critical power projection for the Marine Corps, using its heavy payload capacity to leapfrog ahead of F-35B fighter jets. The KC-130J lands at remote, undeveloped airfields to establish Aviation-Delivered Ground Refueling and re-arming points.

During this self-supported movement, the KC-130J traversed a route from Royal Australian Air Force Base Tindal, Australia, through Cairns, Pohnpei, the Kwajalein Atoll, and Wake Island, terminating in Hawaii. By carrying the necessary maintainers, maintenance equipment, and aviation fuel, the KC-130J allowed the F-35Bs to slingshot deeper into the theater.

"While the jets are focused on the tactical fight, the KC-130J is the workhorse in the background, carrying the maintainers, the maintenance equipment, and the fuel required to dramatically extend the range and lethality of those jets," said 1st Lt. Christian Schwien, a KC-130J co-pilot.

Transforming the KC-130J into a moving, forward logistics hub requires precise integration across the crew. Pilots execute long-range over-water navigation and land the 135,000-pound aircraft on austere strips. In the cargo hold, loadmasters manage weight, balance, and high-stress air-delivered ground refueling operations.

The KC-130J remains positioned to support the missions of tomorrow whether they be winking amidst a sea of blue to the east in the Indo-Pacific or concentrated down under from Australia. In an era where near-peer dynamics and global geopolitics continue to evolve, 3d MAW’s need endures for a versatile platform, one capable of unlocking future operational possibilities while honoring the legacy of aviation feats that define its historic past.

items.title: Bittersweet departure: Nellis’ last A-10 clears runway for future of close air support
items.author: SSgt Kristal Munguia
items.summary: The last A-10 Thunderbolt II aircraft assigned to Nellis Air Force Base, Nevada, made its final departure Sept. 22.
items.body:
NELLIS AIR FORCE BASE, Nev -- The last A-10 Thunderbolt II aircraft assigned to Nellis Air Force Base, Nevada, made its final departure Sept. 22.

Nearly 70 Airmen from Nellis AFB lined up on the flight line to give the A-10, affectionately nicknamed the “Warthog,” one final salute as it took off.

Although the departure signifies the conclusion of nearly 50 years of elite tactical training, operational testing and maintenance sustainability at the installation, the A-10's impact will not soon be forgotten.

The first attack jet arrived at the base in 1977. Over the past five decades, the installation served as the primary proving ground for the Warthog's tactical employment. Nellis-based units refined the aircraft's software, avionics and precision weapons, while the U.S. Air Force Weapons School’s 66th Weapons Squadron trained more than 300 A-10 weapons officers across 100 classes.

“We are maintaining the culture of the A-10 by involving as many other fighter communities involved in the close air support mission,” said Lt. Col. Ridge Flick, the 66th WPS commander. “We are also training F-15 Eagle, F-35 Lightning II and F-16 Fighting Falcon pilots to take on some roles we have had in combat search and rescue.”

While the aircraft itself is departing, Flick emphasized the squadron’s mission of forging elite tactical leaders remains unchanged. The unit will continue training the next generation of ground-based specialists, including combat rescue officers, pararescue, special tactics officers and combat controllers.

As the Air Force retires the A-10 fleet, the military's close air support capability is not declining. Instead, foundational tactical expertise, operational roles and personnel are transitioning to multirole and advanced fighter platforms across the service.

Airmen from the 757th Aircraft Maintenance Squadron's Thunder Aircraft Maintenance Unit are being reassigned to other squadrons and airframes, such as the F-35 and the F-16. The discipline that A-10 maintainers developed over 50 years of managing airframe fatigue, wing replacements and depot-level overhauls is being integrated into those newer flight line programs.

At the same time, fifth-generation platforms like the F-35 are absorbing new close air support and combat search-and-rescue command roles into their operational profiles. The platform combines stealth features, advanced sensor suites and secure data-sharing networks to conduct precision ground-support missions in contested environments. For maintainers making the shift, the transition carries both operational and personal significance.

“Working on the A-10 is meaningful to me because that is something that I share with my grandfather,” said Staff Sgt. Eva Kehn, a 757th AMXS weapons load crew chief. “I’m very excited to have that new chapter and bond over that again with my grandfather.”

With her reassignment to an F-35 unit at Nellis, that unique family connection will continue. Her grandfather now serves as a civilian F-35 instructor, meaning their shared professional bond will simply transition to a new airframe.

“It’s a bittersweet moment,” said Master Sgt. Aaron Edmonds, a 757th AMXS aircraft section chief regarding the A-10 final salute. “I enjoyed my time with the A-10, but I’m excited because this departure marks the closing of one chapter and the start of another.”

For Edmonds, the transition is also a homecoming. After maintaining the F-16 earlier in his career, he spent the last five years working on the A-10 flight line and is eager to bring that seasoned experience back to the Fighting Falcon.

“The advice I would give Airmen who are transitioning from one airframe to another is to be open minded, willing to learn, and carry on the great work ethic from your previous aircraft over to your new one,” Edmonds said.

Although the A-10's engines have gone quiet at Nellis, the tactical DNA forged over five decades of service remains hardwired into the flight line. The transition marks less of a retirement and more of an evolution, ensuring that the Warthog’s legendary commitment to protecting troops on the ground is carried forward by the Airmen and advanced platforms shaping the future fight.

items.title: NORAD and Allied Forces Integrate Airpower During Operation ARCTIC VANGUARD
items.author: Alaskan Command Public Affairs
items.summary: North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD), Danish and NATO forces are conducting combined air defense training during Operation ARCTIC VANGUARD (OAV) 26-4.2, integrating fighters, aerial refueling and airborne command and control to strengthen the defense of North America’s northern approaches.
items.body:
JOINT BASE ELMENDORF-RICHARDSON, Alaska — North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD), Danish and NATO forces are conducting combined air defense training during Operation ARCTIC VANGUARD (OAV) 26-4.2, integrating fighters, aerial refueling and airborne command and control to strengthen the defense of North America’s northern approaches.

NORAD fighter aircraft are operating from Goose Bay, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada, alongside aerial refueling and search and rescue aircraft operating from Bagotville, Québec. This combined activity extends to Keflavik, Iceland, where Royal Danish Air Force fighters and a CL-604 Challenger are participating in training scenarios and air activity alongside a French multirole tanker transport aircraft and NATO airborne warning and control aircraft.

Aircrews are planning and executing defensive counterair training missions focused on integrating allied fighters against advanced simulated air threats. The missions emphasize tactical data sharing and secure communications to exchange information and coordinate actions among participating forces.

This week, NORAD aircraft also joined Danish aircraft at Kangerlussuaq, Greenland, for ground refueling. Planners synchronized fighter arrivals from separate operating locations with tanker and airborne warning and control support while supporting aircraft remained overhead until the fighters were airborne - demonstrating the coordination required to sustain combined air operations across the Arctic.

“We welcome NORAD forces to the region and value the experience and capabilities they bring to our combined operations,” said Maj. Gen. Jan Dam, chief of the Royal Danish Air Force. “Operating together in the air and on the ground builds the trust and coordination we need to strengthen our shared security in the Arctic.”

Operation ARCTIC VANGUARD is a long-planned NORAD operation and part of a recurring series of Arctic operations to strengthen forward presence and defend North America’s northern approaches. While some iterations of Operation ARCTIC VANGUARD are led and conducted by U.S. Northern Command (USNORTHCOM), both NORAD and USNORTHCOM OAVs support the NORAD and USNORTHCOM Nordic Bridge concept, which aligns Arctic operations, exercises and training activities with those of NATO, individual nations, and regional partners.

items.title: 2026 Virtual DCSA Security Conference Focuses on “Protect Our Potential” Through Partnership, Modernization and Mission Readiness
items.author: John Joyce
items.summary: QUANTICO, Va. — The Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) hosted the 2026 Virtual DCSA Security Conference Sept. 14-18, as cleared industry professionals, Department of War (DoW) security stakeholders and foreign ownership, control or influence (FOCI) practitioners convened under the shared theme, “Protect Our Potential.” DCSA combined its annual National Insider Threat Awareness Month Conference, Security Conference for Industry, Security Conference for DoW, and FOCI Conference
items.body: QUANTICO, Va. — The Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) hosted the 2026 Virtual DCSA Security Conference Sept. 14-18, as cleared industry professionals, Department of War (DoW) security stakeholders and foreign ownership, control or influence (FOCI) practitioners convened under the shared theme, “Protect Our Potential.” DCSA combined its annual National Insider Threat Awareness Month Conference, Security Conference for Industry, Security Conference for DoW, and FOCI Conference into a single week to streamline information sharing, strengthen collaboration, and familiarize participants with DCSA’s Strategic Execution Plan to deliver data-driven, threat-informed, and customer-trusted security services at scale. “Government and industry must work together at the speed of operations to secure our vital national interests,” said DCSA Chief of Staff Jeffrey Sgarlata as the conference opened on Sept. 14 for the industry-focused sessions. “If industry cannot move at pace, the warfighter loses.” Sgarlata urged government and industry to meet emerging security challenges together and emphasized that the security enterprise cannot permit process, uncertainty or unnecessary delay to hinder the delivery of trusted capability to the warfighter. “Government and industry need each other to meet evolving security challenges,” said Ike Rivers, NISPPAC Industry spokesperson. “DCSA brings the oversight perspective, while industry brings the implementation perspective. Sustained communication, clarity and collaboration are essential to turn security requirements into effective practices that protect the nation’s most critical capabilities.” Rivers was among more than 60 speakers presenting briefs and technical updates while answering questions throughout the conference. Speakers emphasized the importance of defending sensitive information, technology and facilities while enabling the people, partnerships and capabilities that give the United States a sustained competitive advantage. “The DCSA Security Conference strengthened relationships across DCSA security disciplines and with our cleared industry partners, fostering the information sharing and collaboration essential to our shared mission,” said David Scott, DCSA associate director for Industrial Security. “I really appreciated the outstanding participation from our speakers and the more than 3,000 virtual participants who joined us each day. This level of engagement demonstrates the enduring value of the government-industry partnership.” Participants engaged with DCSA and DoW subject matter experts on National Industrial Security Program operations, cleared-industry and entity-vetting updates, workforce development, Trusted Workforce 2.0 and adjudications. Discussions also examined insider-threat assessment and threat management, the weaponization of artificial intelligence, National Industrial Security System–Increment II (NI2) updates and other emerging challenges shaping today’s security environment. Beginning Sept. 16, the DoW portion of the conference focused on DCSA capabilities, tools and partnerships supporting readiness across the department’s components. Sessions addressed adjudications, NISP compliance and system updates, artificial intelligence and machine learning in the insider-threat domain, contracting awareness, personnel vetting, security considerations related to mental health, customer success, and the integration of operations security with security stakeholders. Moreover, participants identified security policy and vetting considerations related to mission readiness and shared feedback on National Background Investigation Services (NBIS) adoption and security workforce training needs. While closing the DoW portion of the conference on Sept. 18, DCSA Chief Operating Officer Blake Moore emphasized the agency’s mission-enablement focus. “We are mission enablers, and that is how we see ourselves,” said DCSA Chief Operating Officer Blake Moore. “The question is no longer whether we can say ‘yes,’ but how fast we can say ‘yes’ securely. Our standard moving forward is speed, transparency, accountability and results – delivering capability at the speed the warfighter needs.” The conference aligned with DCSA’s Strategic Execution Plan, which prioritizes delivery of NBIS; deployment of NI2; modernization of trusted-workforce determinations; rebuilding the workforce compact; customer-centric operations; and audit-ready integration and efficiency through artificial intelligence. For participants, those priorities reflected DCSA’s commitment to modernize the systems and processes supporting the trusted workforce and the Defense Industrial Base. DCSA’s leadership principles – empowered ownership, urgency, accountability, customer focus and candid communication – provide the operating approach for delivering that modernization at mission speed and strengthening trust with mission partners. The conference concluded after five days of discussions focused on confronting evolving security challenges, sharing mission-relevant information and sustaining the partnerships necessary to protect the people, technology and industrial capabilities that underpin national defense.

items.title: Joint Press Release: US, Indonesia Co-chair Largest ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting (ADMM)-Plus Exercise in a Decade with the Participation of 2,200 Personnel from 19 Countries
items.author: SFC Timothy Hughes
items.summary: The United States participates in first of its kind Exercise Trident Resolve 2026 is a major multinational disaster-response exercise in Banten, Indonesia, bringing together around 2,200 military and civilian personnel from all 19 ADMM-Plus countries. The exercise focuses on strengthening cooperation in humanitarian assistance, disaster relief, military medicine and cybersecurity through simulated search-and-rescue, medical evacuation, hazardous-material response, infrastructure repair and marit
items.body:
Joint press release courtesy of multinational ASEAN ADMM Plus public affairs offices.

BANTEN, Indonesia -- About 2,200 personnel from the militaries of all 19 ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting (ADMM)-Plus countries and civilian agencies are participating in Exercise Trident Resolve (XTR), held in Banten, Indonesia from 20 to 26 September 2026. XTR is the first ADMM-Plus Combined Field Training Exercise (FTX) involving three Experts’ Working Groups (EWGs) – Cyber Security (CS), Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR) and Military Medicine (MM), and the largest ADMM-Plus exercise in a decade by personnel participation.

Conducted across seven distributed sites and at sea, XTR will exercise participating militaries’ and civilian agencies’ coordination and response to a large-scale disaster, through activities spanning search and rescue; medical evacuation and treatment; chemical, biological and radiological response; and infrastructure repair. As part of XTR’s maritime component, Indonesia’s hospital ship KRI dr. Soeharso and Singapore’s Landing Ship Tank RSS Endeavour with surgical capabilities onboard a Rapidly Deployable Maritime Container will complement shore-based medical facilities and expand the range of medical facilities to treat simulated casualties. XTR also marks the first FTX of the ADMM-Plus EWG on Cyber Security, with cybersecurity activities focused on protecting information systems and information integrity against disruption or compromise during the multinational disaster response.

As part of XTR’s activities, participating militaries and civilian agencies will also support local communities in Banten through selected medical, public health and infrastructure activities, led by Indonesian authorities and local partners.

On 22 September, ASEAN Defence Senior Officials' Meeting (ADSOM) Leaders and senior defense officials from participating countries visited XTR and observed the exercise activities. Lieutenant General Rui F.G.P. Duarte, Inspector General of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Indonesia, said, “Exercise Trident Resolve represents an important milestone in practical cooperation between the ASEAN and Plus countries, under the ADMM-Plus framework. Beyond it’s operational objectives, this exercise also strengthens trust and friendship amongst participating countries.”

XTR is hosted by Indonesia and jointly organized by the co-chairs of the three ADMM-Plus EWGs: Australia and Cambodia for CS, Singapore and New Zealand for HADR, and Indonesia and the United States for MM. Established in 2010, the ADMM-Plus remains the region’s principal platform for practical defense cooperation among its member countries.

items.title: PACOM Mortuary Affairs Symposium Strengthens Readiness Across the Pacific
items.author: SSG Egypt Johnson
items.summary: FORT SHAFTER, Hawaii— U.S. Army Pacific (USARPAC) G4 Mortuary Affairs team hosted the PACOM Mortuary Affairs Symposium at headquarters, Sept. 14-18, bringing together Mortuary Affairs professionals, Department of War and Joint personnel, and Partner Nation representatives to identify readiness gaps, examine emerging requirements and develop solutions for Mortuary Affairs operations in large-scale combat operations.
items.body: FORT SHAFTER, Hawaii— U.S. Army Pacific (USARPAC) G4 Mortuary Affairs team hosted the PACOM Mortuary Affairs Symposium at headquarters, Sept. 14-18, bringing together Mortuary Affairs professionals, Department of War and Joint personnel, and Partner Nation representatives to identify readiness gaps, examine emerging requirements and develop solutions for Mortuary Affairs operations in large-scale combat operations. The weeklong symposium focused on Army tactical-level Mortuary Affairs readiness, unit recovery team modernization, expeditionary preservation of human remains, and autonomous search and recovery capabilities. “We identified significant tactical readiness shortfalls,” said Master Sgt. Dimitry Razell, USARPAC Senior Mortuary Affairs noncommissioned officer. “Across the force, our Four Victor personnel are not fully trained for their positions.” The symposium also highlighted the need to expand the theater’s ability to preserve human remains in an expeditionary environment. “Expeditionary preservation of human remains is a key requirement for the theater,” Razell said. “We need to purchase, manufacture and pre-position that equipment at our theater Mortuary Affairs points.” Razell said the capability will also be critical in Okinawa to ensure Mortuary Affairs forces can support operations throughout the region. The symposium provided an opportunity for participants to examine current capabilities, identify gaps and synchronize modernization efforts across the Mortuary Affairs enterprise. “Our modernization and innovation priorities focus on equipment modernization, expeditionary capabilities, autonomous and emerging technologies, and interoperability with partners,” Razell said. Moving forward, the enterprise will focus on closing training shortfalls, prioritizing expeditionary embalming capabilities at theater Mortuary Affairs points and in Okinawa, accelerating MACRS redevelopment, and resourcing additional MORTS devices throughout the theater. The symposium reinforced the importance of maintaining a ready, adaptable Mortuary Affairs enterprise capable of supporting Soldiers and commanders across the Pacific during competition, crisis and large-scale combat operations. As the Army prepares for the demands of the modern battlefield, Mortuary Affairs professionals across the Pacific are identifying gaps today, modernizing capabilities for tomorrow, and ensuring the Army is prepared to honor and care for its fallen wherever the mission takes them.

items.title: A Legacy of Dual Service: Maj. Gen. Michael C. Thompson inducted into Oklahoma National Guard OCS Hall of Fame
items.author: Leanna Maschino
items.summary: OKLAHOMA CITY - When Maj. Gen. Michael C. Thompson entered the Oklahoma Army National Guard as an enlisted Soldier in 1983, he embarked on a military career that would span nearly four decades and take him from the ranks of an enlisted Soldier to the highest levels of military leadership in Oklahoma.
items.body:
OKLAHOMA CITY - When Maj. Gen. Michael C. Thompson entered the Oklahoma Army National Guard as an enlisted Soldier in 1983, he embarked on a military career that would span nearly four decades and take him from the ranks of an enlisted Soldier to the highest levels of military leadership in Oklahoma.

Thompson’s lifelong commitment to duty, organizational excellence, and the welfare of Soldiers was recognized as he was formally inducted into the Oklahoma National Guard Officer Candidate School (OCS) Hall of Fame during a ceremony held Sunday, Sept. 20, 2026, at the Oklahoma National Guard Museum in Oklahoma City.

“I appreciate the significance of today’s event, but the true honor for me was to wear our country’s uniform for so many years,” Thompson said. “The Oklahoma National Guard has benefited me and my family for years to come.”

A graduate of OCS Class 31, Thompson earned his commission Aug. 2, 1986, pinning on the gold bars of a second lieutenant and officially beginning his commissioned service as an infantry platoon leader with Company A, 2nd Battalion, 180th Infantry Regiment in Oklahoma City.

That first tactical assignment marked the beginning of a 38-year career defined by increasing responsibility and service at the state and national levels, culminating in his role as the Adjutant General for Oklahoma, followed by Special Assistant to the Chief of the National Guard Bureau in Washington, D.C.

Throughout his commissioned service, Thompson developed a reputation as a commander who led from the front, taking on assignments of increasing scope and responsibility. As commander of the 1st Battalion, 279th Infantry Regiment, he led critical humanitarian relief and security operations in New Orleans in the immediate aftermath of Hurricane Katrina, helping provide stability and support to American citizens during one of the nation’s worst natural disasters.

Later, during Operation Iraqi Freedom, Thompson commanded a security force unit in combat, leading the first infantry formation from Oklahoma to be awarded the Combat Infantry Badge since the Korean War.

Following battalion command, Thompson led 90th Troop Command as brigade commander. In 2012, he was promoted to brigadier general, assuming the roles of Land Component Commander and Assistant Adjutant General for the Oklahoma Army National Guard.

In 2017, Thompson was appointed by the Governor to serve as The Adjutant General of Oklahoma. As the state’s senior military leader, he served as principal military advisor to the commander-in-chief and commanded both the Oklahoma Army and Air National Guard through 2021, overseeing force mobilizations, modernization efforts, and domestic emergency operations.

Thompson’s service as a Citizen-Soldier extended well beyond the National Guard. During his 25-year career with the Oklahoma Highway Patrol, he rose from road trooper to Commissioner of the Oklahoma Department of Public Safety. In April 1995, he was among the first responders at the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building following the Oklahoma City bombing, an experience that became part of a career dedicated to protecting Oklahomans during some of the state’s most challenging moments.

That experience in public safety leadership eventually led to his appointment to the Governor’s Cabinet as Oklahoma Secretary of Safety and Security, while also serving as Commissioner of the Oklahoma Department of Public Safety.

Balancing two demanding careers, Thompson also pursued academic excellence. He earned a Bachelor of Science from Langston University, a Master of Science from Oklahoma State University, and a Master of Strategic Studies from the United States Army War College. He also graduated from the FBI National Academy in Quantico, Virginia.

Behind Thompson’s decades of service is a family who shared in the sacrifices that came with it, including his wife of 42 years, whose support remained constant through the demands and challenges of his career. Their two sons also served in the U.S. military, continuing a family tradition of service that now spans generations.

“I couldn’t imagine any of this without the unwavering support of my family, close and extended,” Thompson said. “Family is everything. My wife, Debbie, and I have been married 42 years and she is my rock. I am proud of my sons for understanding the sacrifices of serving and ultimately serving in our U.S. Army as well.”

For Thompson, the OCS Hall of Fame induction represents a return to where his commissioned military career began. As Class 31’s most distinguished alumnus, his career offers a tangible example of where the foundation built at Officer Candidate School can lead: from a second lieutenant leading an infantry platoon to the highest levels of military and public service in Oklahoma.

His record of military leadership, combat service, law enforcement, and public service now becomes part of the history carried forward by the candidates who follow.

“As a young man I never dreamed where my commission from Officer Candidate School would take me,” Thompson said. “It was an incredible journey that I will always cherish.”

In addition to his military honors, Thompson is a member of the Oklahoma Law Enforcement Hall of Fame and also has been inducted into the Oklahoma State University Hall of Fame.

items.title: September MCAS New River Go-Getter
items.author: LCpl Chloe Lewczyk
items.summary: MARINE CORPS BASE CAMP LEJEUNE, N.C. – U.S. Marine Corps Sgt. Ashton J. Hmielewski, a formal school instructor for MV-22 Avionics at Center for Naval Aviation Technical Training Unit New River, has been recognized as the Go-Getter for September 2026.
items.body:
A native of Duluth, Minnesota, who was raised in River Falls, Wisconsin, Hmielewski enlisted in the Marine Corps in 2020 as the nation entered the COVID-19 pandemic. He was part of the first company to complete recruit training under pandemic restrictions before continuing through Marine Combat Training, aviation electronics “A” school in Pensacola, Florida, and training at Center for Naval Aviation Technical Training Unit (CNATTU) New River as a student.

After completing the training pipeline, Hmielewski was stationed at Marine Corps Base Hawaii for four years, where he supported two Marine Rotational Force–Darwin rotations and earned several qualifications within his work center. He later received orders to CNATTU New River, where he has served as an instructor for over a year.

“I never really had a concrete calling to the Marines, but I knew I always wanted to serve in the Armed Forces,” said Hmielewski. “When I was 17, I called every branch’s recruiting office on a Saturday night around 2300, and whatever recruiter got back to me first was the branch I’d join. Naturally the Marines called me back within about 20 minutes. I wanted the best; to put it bluntly, I chose correctly.”

As a formal schoolhouse instructor, Hmielewski is responsible for preparing students with the technical knowledge and professional foundation necessary to succeed in the fleet.

"Sergeant Hmielewski has been an asset to the command by being an outstanding lead instructor who conducted two classes to completion resulting in 11 graduations with an average GPA of 95.97 providing Fleet ready maintainers to the Navy and Marine Corps V-22 platforms,” said Capt. Steven Meyer, operations officer, CNATTU New River.

Hmielewski’s approach to instruction centers on the individual Marine. He adapts lessons to accommodate different learning styles, shifting between hands-on training, classroom instruction, visual aids and diagrams as needed. Beyond technical training, he strives to mentor students on the aircraft, fleet Marine Corps and life beyond the classroom.

“As an instructor, our job is to instill into our students the knowledge required to succeed, but also to serve as a mentor,” said Hmielewski. “For me, I attempt to focus on the individual and cater toward their learning style.”

For Hmielewski, the most rewarding part of the job is hearing that former students are succeeding in the fleet. Their performance provides both a source of pride and an opportunity to improve the instruction he provides for future classes.

“The best part is hearing how well my students are doing in the fleet, Marine Corps or Navy and being able to reflect on what shortcomings they may have to better improve my current students,” he said. “In short, giving back to the fleet by creating a maintainer who excels and knows what they do.”

Although he acknowledges the challenge of balancing student needs, physical fitness, mental welfare and course objectives, Hmielewski views improvement as an everyday responsibility. He remains motivated by the opportunity to make each lesson, day, week and class better than the last.

“The motivation to get up and go comes down to the question I ask myself every day: what else could you do that could be better?” said Hmielewski. “For most every day, that is to go out, do more than what is expected, and rest again that same night knowing you gave it all you had.”

Outside of his primary job as a formal schoolhouse instructor, Hmielewski also takes on the role of the unit readiness coordinator, where he manages 460 family care plans and ensures 100% compliance and deployable readiness; while increasing command morale by conducting fundraising events for two major command events. He is also actively pursuing a degree in electrical engineering through ECPI University.

Through his commitment to mentorship, technical excellence and continuous improvement, Hmielewski exemplifies the go-getter mindset and helps ensure the next generation of MV-22 avionics maintainers is ready to support the fleet.

items.title: Experts: Affordable Munitions Could Help USAF in Taiwan Conflict, but More Is Needed
items.author: Todd South
items.summary: A new think tank report calls for a buildup of U.S. drones and munitions needed for a potential fight against the Chinese military over Taiwan, thought other experts argue the report is missing some nuance in the munitions equation. The post Experts: Affordable Munitions Could Help USAF in Taiwan Conflict, but More Is Needed appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

A new think tank report calls for a buildup of U.S. drones and munitions needed for a potential fight against the Chinese military over Taiwan, thought other experts argue the report is missing some nuance in the munitions equation.

The Center for a New American Security’s report, “Drones, Missiles, and the U.S. Munitions Shortage: The Role of Affordable Mass in a Taiwan Conflict,” released Sept. 18, makes the case for increased long-range weapons to strike Chinese military targets to thwart a takeover of Taiwan.

The report, authored by Philip Sheers and Stacie Pettyjohn, notes a gap between the number of targets the U.S. would need to strike and its diminishing stockpiles, given the ongoing use of such weapons in the conflict with Iran.

“In a U.S.-China conflict over Taiwan that is likely to become protracted, the inventory depth and disruption that lower-cost systems can provide will be invaluable to reversing U.S. disadvantages and stopping China from achieving its operational objectives,” Sheers and Pettyjohn write.

To close the gap, the report recommends both stockpiling high-end missiles and massing cheap drones and munitions to overwhelm a Chinese attack. Other recommendations include:

Multiyear funding and contracts so manufacturers can expand weapons production capacity and the Pentagon can rebuild long-range missile stores

Funding for cheap, long-range anti-ship and land-attack weapons to quickly fill inventory gaps.

Standardized shared components across airframes to lower costs and scale production.

Pairing inexpensive drones with advanced missiles to drain enemy air defenses.

Prioritizing easily built designs rather than over-engineering

Routing updates and briefings to Congress on these issues

The White House and Pentagon have taken steps to boost munitions production this year, especially low-cost weapons.

In July, the Pentagon announced multiyear framework agreements with Anduril, CoAspire, and Zone 5 Technologies to mass-produce missiles for the Air Force, followed by a Sept. 17 announcement that Lockheed Martin would expand production of the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile.

The former announcement is part of USAF’s Family of Affordable Mass Missiles program, unveiled in the fiscal 2026 budget with plans to ramp up such production to hit 5,300 missiles a year by 2028 and reach nearly 8,000 missiles a year by 2031.

The current projected five-year budget for FAMM is more than $12 billion for nearly 27,000 missiles.

Retired Air Force Col. Mark Gunzinger , now with AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the CNAS report’s call for more munitions is necessary. But he cautioned that the report’s focus on making weapons affordable needs to be tweaked.

“It should not be about buying cheaper weapons; it should be about how to optimize cost per effect in the battlespace,” Gunzinger said.

The Air Force must fight asymmetrically and maximize the effect of each strike, regardless of munition or platform, and there’s a middle ground for weapons and platform development and procurement, Gunzinger argued.

Precision-guided, specialized weapons such as the Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile and the platforms that deliver them are pricey, and lower-end, short-range munitions for stationary targets have their place, but Gunzinger said defense planners can often make too much of a tradeoff if they focus too much on price to the detriment of capability.

“Now you’ve got something that, ‘OK, you hit a price point, but is it going to survive long enough to do its mission?’” Gunzinger said. “Is it going to be able to shoot its weapon before it dies?”

A Numbers Game

The CNAS report’s operational and tactical focus is countering a People’s Liberation Army attack on Taiwan with strikes against PLA ships—destroyers and amphibious assault ships—and hitting airfields on the periphery of the country, close to the Taiwan Strait.

But it does not include a plan to hit the Chinese mainland interior.

“The paper focuses on denying a PLA joint island landing campaign without considering strategic attacks to deny sanctuaries to the PLA and collapse China’s ability to maintain the offensive,” Gunzinger said. “This risks reducing a conflict with the PLA over Taiwan to a force-on-force math problem, like how many weapons and aircraft are needed to attack PLA forces located in the Taiwan Strait and coastal China. It risks becoming a numbers game.”

Because striking mainland China in a Taiwan invasion scenario might be required, Gunzinger said the current 500-nautical-mile limit of most affordable strike options undermines the CNAS report’s conclusion that more mass will equate to victory.

“China has the capability to project outer and inner rings of airborne and sea-based air defense sensors and shooters to defend its cross-Strait forces and operations,” Gunzinger said.

And using nonstealthy drones to approach the Chinese coastline to then launch affordable missiles doesn’t work either, he said. “This would likely result in losses of the aircraft and their weapons.”

“We win part of the battle,” Gunzinger said. “They win the war.”

Breaking a Stalemate

The numbers-on-numbers approach is what has led to a stalemate in the Russia-Ukraine War, said retired Navy Cmdr. J. Michael Dahm , now a senior fellow for aerospace and China studies at Mitchell.

“Just because you can generate mass doesn’t mean that you’re going to achieve your effects,” Dahm told Air & Space Forces Magazine. “You may be able to keep your adversary off balance, but if you’re not going to then judo throw him into what you want him to do, you’re just engaging in this kind of protracted, endless warfare.”

Throughout the history of the modern Chinese military, it has mostly been defense-oriented, Dahm said. The PLA has airfields dotting its landscape and hardened sites to pull and rotate forces from, as well as a layered air defense network.

What could overwhelm the Chinese defenses, however, is what the U.S. has seen poke through its defenses recently in the Middle East, Dahm said. Iranian air attacks have used a combination of low-end munitions and cheap drones with more expensive and capable missiles fired from various angles, locations, and at varying rates of speed to confuse and defeat air defenses.

This aligns with one of the report’s recommendations—for the Pentagon to develop new operational concepts that pair cheap and high-end weapons for mixed attacks.

“Using low-cost drones in the opening wave to identify air defenses, consume interceptors, and relay targeting data to follow-on missiles offers a promising and sustainable way to create repeated air base disruption,” according to the report. “High-end weapons should be preserved for more challenging targets, while affordable mass should be integrated into strike plans to service soft targets and to saturate air defenses.”

“The Iranians have figured out how to be effective: … send a whole bunch of slow-moving drones with a couple of cruise missiles and a couple of ballistic missiles,” Dahm said.

That’s because modern air defenders must set their systems to track certain ranges, altitudes, and speeds of whatever is in the airspace. And they can’t track everything effectively all at once.

“I don’t want a flock of birds showing up on my radar, so I set the speed gate for higher speed, but how high do I set it for? 100 knots or do I set it for Mach 3? What am I looking for? Range. How far am I looking? Altitude. Am I looking high? Am I looking low?” Dahm said.

Those factors mean an air defense system can’t stop everything.

“The way you overwhelm even the most sophisticated air defense system is you send some slow stuff, you send some medium stuff, and then you send these ballistic missiles that are screaming in from the upper atmosphere at Mach 3-4-5,” Dahm said. “It is hard for any modern air defense system to deal with all those inputs.”

While Iran is using that method against the U.S., Dahm advocates the U.S. use the same strategy in a Taiwan scenario against the PLA.

“That is absolutely what we should be doing,” Dahm said.

For example, to strike a Chinese military ship, such as a cruiser, Dahm said U.S. or coalition countries wouldn’t only send the same type of missile from one direction. They would simultaneously target the ship from air, land, sea, and subsurface platforms with a variety of projectiles at varying speeds and ranges, though the centerpiece of the assault might be an LRASM.

“You might send two LRASMs, but you need to accompany that with some of these more cost-effective missiles,” he said. “It is the reason we need the cost-effectiveness and the affordability, because we shouldn’t have an expectation that all of those weapons are going to work.”

items.title: U.S. Forces Combine Approaches During Joint Airfield Damage Repair Training
items.author: SGT Deneisha Owens-McParland
items.summary: Joint Airfield Damage Repair training brought together U.S. Soldiers, U.S. Marines and U.S. Airmen at Marine Corps Training Area Bellows, Hawaii, Sept. 14-18, 2026, to strengthen the joint force’s ability to assess and repair damaged airfields throughout the Indo-Pacific.
items.body:
MARINE CORPS TRAINING AREA BELLOWS, Hawaii — Joint Airfield Damage Repair training brought together U.S. Soldiers, U.S. Marines and U.S. Airmen at Marine Corps Training Area Bellows, Hawaii, Sept. 14-18, 2026, to strengthen the joint force’s ability to assess and repair damaged airfields throughout the Indo-Pacific.

Soldiers from the 523rd Engineer Support Company and 70th Clearance Company trained alongside Marines from Marine Wing Support Squadron 174 and Airmen from the 647th Civil Engineer Squadron throughout the weeklong exercise. Joint teams assessed and marked simulated damage across the airfield before working to repair simulated craters and restore the damaged surfaces.

While each service brought its own procedures, equipment and experience to the mission, the training provided an opportunity to put those approaches side by side, share expertise and work toward a more integrated approach to airfield damage repair.

“We spent around two to three months coordinating over a series of joint exercises, as well as rehearsals and training meetings, to ensure that all partners got something out of this culminating exercise and were able to kind of marry their separate concepts of how to do airfield damage repair together,” said 2nd Lt. Alok Barua, 1st Platoon, 523rd Engineer Support Company, 84th Engineer Battalion, 130th Engineer Brigade.

Beyond completing the repairs, participants had the opportunity to become familiar with equipment and techniques used by their joint partners.

“Our joint training has consisted of us assisting each other with equipment,” said Sgt. Jacob Teegarden, 1st Platoon, 523rd Engineer Support Company, 84th Engineer Battalion, 130th Engineer Brigade. “They operate different equipment, and so it allows us to get some good training on different branches, what their equipment is.”

Equipment was only one part of the exchange. Each service also brought its own methods for clearing and repairing airfield damage, giving the joint teams a chance to see those different approaches in practice.

“This exercise kind of allowed us to integrate with the Army and the Air Force and learn from their specific ways that they do their clearances and their repairs,” said 2nd Lt. Zachary Kolb, Marine Wing Support Squadron 174. “Our Marines and Airmen and Soldiers kind of learn from each other, so we can bring it back to our own units.”

Integrating the services also meant learning how to communicate across differences in terminology and procedures.

“In a real-world environment, we need to be able to communicate clearly and understand each other’s language,” said 2nd Lt. Joshua Kent, 647th Civil Engineer Squadron. “There are different terms we use in each service that I think are good for everybody to experience here in a training environment before we go into the real world and operate. It allows us to operate more quickly and more efficiently.”

As the week progressed, participants moved from rehearsals and dry iterations into live airfield damage repair, increasing the pace as they became more familiar with working together.

For the Army, bringing those capabilities together also helped further develop how its approach to airfield damage repair can complement established Air Force and Marine Corps practices. Barua said the services bring different capabilities to the mission, from technical expertise in airfield construction and repair to lighter, rapidly deployable methods suited for expeditionary operations.

Rather than eliminating those differences, the training allowed the services to better understand how their individual capabilities, procedures and equipment can work together during a joint response.

“Bringing together our standard operating procedures and their doctrine — all the way down to our guys working on their equipment, getting to know each other and building those relationships that really are going to matter in a conflict in the Pacific — that has been really exciting,” Barua said. “It has made me very confident that America stands ready to conduct airfield damage repair if a contingency should happen in the Pacific theater.”

items.title: US Navy destroyers tested in Middle East as demands mount
items.author: Natalie Oliverio
items.summary: The concentration of Navy destroyers in the Middle East raises questions about meeting sustained operational demand.
items.body:
Naval

US Navy destroyers tested in Middle East as demands mount

Arleigh Burke-class USS Carney (U.S. Navy)

Navy destroyers are concentrated in the Middle East as U.S. forces conduct operations against Iran, according to U.S. Central Command — a move that puts renewed operational demands on a fleet that has experienced prolonged maintenance periods.

As of Sept. 14, two Navy guided-missile destroyers were operating in the Red Sea and another 13 were in the Arabian Sea, according to the U.S. Naval Institute’s fleet tracker , which uses both Navy and public data.

The Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS Stout also departed Naval Station Norfolk on Monday to begin deployment operations after months of training, maintenance and certification events, according to Naval Surface Force Atlantic.

The demand facing the class has been significant, even before the start of the Iran war.

The USS Carney spent 235 days deployed from September 2023 to May 2024 and conducted 51 engagements against Houthi-launched weapons, according to the Navy . The campaign demonstrated what operations around one of those chokepoints can demand from destroyers.

When USS Carney returned in May 2024, then-Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Lisa Franchetti told the crew that the last time the Navy had directly engaged an enemy to that degree was during World War II .

The renewed demand for destroyers in the Middle East comes as the Navy’s maintenance system has struggled to keep the fleet on schedule.

U.S. Fleet Forces Command declined to discuss its current destroyer readiness posture, current operations or potential effects on future deployment schedules, citing operational-security and classification guidelines. The command also declined to provide historical aggregate data on destroyer operational tempo.

According to a December 2025 Congressional Budget Office analysis of Navy maintenance data, the Arleigh Burke-class destroyer overhauls that began between 2011 and 2024 took an average of 26% longer than the Navy’s final schedules estimated.

The 225 DDG-51 overhauls CBO analyzed also required 8% more labor than scheduled.

CBO projected that DDG-51 destroyers will spend an average of more than nine years, or about 27% of their planned service lives, in maintenance. That is more than twice the roughly four years envisioned in the Navy’s 2012 class maintenance plans.

The federal budget agency identified several factors contributing to longer maintenance periods, including the aging fleet, postponed maintenance, late inspections and contract awards, unexpected additional work, delays in parts and materials and modernization work.

The average age of the DDG-51 fleet rose from 10 years in 2011 to 20 years in 2024.

The Government Accountability Office has found broader problems across the Navy’s conventional surface fleet.

In a January 2025 review , GAO found that the Navy requested nearly $24.9 billion for combat-surface-ship maintenance from fiscal 2020 through 2023 and reported that nearly $25.9 billion was appropriated. The Navy reported obligating 99.7% of that funding by the end of fiscal 2023. Yet, GAO found that the service continued to face shortages of spare parts, insufficient qualified maintenance personnel and a continuing need to defer maintenance.

CBO’s analysis covers maintenance events beginning in 2011 and points to longstanding factors, including the age of the destroyer fleet and postponed work.

Natalie Oliverio is an independent journalist and Navy veteran who covers military and veterans’ issues. Drawing on her experience as a talent executive and mentor, she writes about the policies, people and programs shaping the military community.
