items.title: Investigators Blame F-16 Thunderbird Crash on Turned Fan Blade Deep in Engine
items.author: Greg Hadley
items.summary: A misaligned vane in an F-16 engine that field-level maintainers cannot see to inspect caused one of the U.S. Air Force's Thunderbird jets to crash last December, a new report concludes. The same problem led another F-16 to crash 20 months earlier. The post Investigators Blame F-16 Thunderbird Crash on Turned Fan Blade Deep in Engine appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

A misaligned vane in an F-16 engine that field-level maintainers cannot see to inspect caused one of the U.S. Air Force’s Thunderbird jets to crash last December, a new report concludes. The same problem led another F-16 to crash 20 months earlier.

The pilots ejected in both cases, escaping with minor injuries, while both jets were total losses. Separate Air Force Accident Investigation Boards came to similar conclusions.

The report on the Dec. 3, 2025, Thunderbird crash in the California desert was released Sept. 21. The report on the prior crash, on April 30, 2024 , near Holloman Air Force Base, N.M., was released months before the Thunderbird crash, in February 2025.

The latest investigation report valued the loss of the Thunderbird F-16 at $33.5 million.

Both accidents were blamed on turned variable vanes deep in the Pratt & Whitney F100-PW-220 engine’s high-pressure compressor. Investigators determined that one or more vanes were turned and misaligned, creating “abnormal aerodynamic forces” and “irregular wake patterns” as air flowed through the engines. The resulting stress on compressor blades caused vanes to break or crack, casuing the engines to “catastrophically” fail.

The Thunderbird investigation report cited three known instances where compressor blades fractured due to turned vanes, but it did not specify a third instance. Besides the Holloman crash in 2024 and the Thunderbird crash in 2025, no publicly released Accident Investigation Board reports from the last decade mention fractured compressor blades in the F100-PW-220.

In both the Holloman and Thunderbird cases, field maintainers failed to catch the misaligned vanes. While some stages can be inspected with a borescope, the fifth stage of the engine core cannot be seen in the F100-PW-220 without completely disassembling the engine core.

Notably, both F-16 engines in question had experienced foreign object debris, or FOD, events in the years prior to the crashes. The Thunderbird jet engine’s FOD event occurred in October 2021, and the Holloman F-16’s FOD event happened in August 2022. In both cases, maintainers noted damage to early stages of the inlet fan but found no issues with the fourth, seventh, or eighth stages, which they could inspect using a borescope.

The Air Force’s technical orders for the F-16 do not require maintainers to remove and disassemble the engine core to inspect those stages after a FOD event if no damage is found in the surrounding stages. It’s unclear if the FOD events caused the vanes to turn, however, so cannot be clearly blamed for triggering the events.

The accident investigation board for the Holloman F-16 crash noted that Pratt & Whitney’s analysis determined the FOD event was the probable cause of the vane turning, but expert opinions varied when asked if it was possible for damage to occur to a later stage if no damage was observed in the ones before it. That left the cause inconclusive.

Similarly, the board for the Thunderbird crash noted that it was “impossible to conclusively determine” what caused the turned vanes. It did, however, note that the lack of inspection for the fifth and sixth stages after a FOD event “substantially contributed to the mishap.”

“The post-FOD event guidance contains an inherent inability to inspect these specific sections of the engine core. Additionally, the core of the engine is only inspected during scheduled maintenance when a core component reaches its overhaul threshold, leaving time for potential damage to progress undetected,” the report states.

A spokesperson for the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center did not immediately comment on whether the technical guidance might be changed to require complete inspections following a FOD event or to trigger other steps to prevent similar mishaps. In February 2025, after the report for the Holloman crash was released, the spokesperson said the center’s F-16 program office “is looking at this issue and is working closely with the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center’s Propulsion Directorate, the engineering authority for the engine, to correct any deficiencies.”

‘Ejecting Was Ultimately the Only Option’

In addition to detailing the engine issues, the Thunderbird report detailed how the pilot did everything possible to save the jet.

An experienced instructor pilot with nearly 1,400 flight hours, the pilot was on a routine training flight working on loops and rolls and flying from the Thunderbirds’ famed “delta formation.” The mishap pilot had planned to peel off from the formation during the loops to avoid exacerbating a stiff neck, then rejoin the formation for the rolls. But as the pilot waited to rejoin, the engine stalled. It felt “like the jet just … stopped midair,” the pilot told investigators.

Seeking to recover, the pilot sacrificed speed to gain altitude, then tried a secondary engine control. When that didn’t work, the pilot attempted an engine restart. “It sounded like things were grinding,” the pilot reported later. Finally, more than four minutes after the engine stalled, the pilot chose to eject.

The Accident Investigation Board concluded that “ejecting was ultimately the only option which provided a favorable outcome.”

Yet the ejection wasn’t flawless—the F-16’s ACES II ejection seat has two hoses that transfer hot gas from the ejection initiators to the sequence valves, and they’re supposed to disconnect automatically during an ejection. One of the hoses in the Thunderbird F-16 didn’t disconnect properly but ripped from the violence of the ejection.

The plane went down near Trone, Calif., a small desert community near Death Valley. Upon impact, debris scattered up to 750 feet away. A local civilian who saw the crash got to the pilot first, and Navy search and rescue responded within minutes to transport for medical care. The pilot was discharged the same day.

items.title: Space Force Seeks Maneuverable Spacecraft for On-Demand Launch
items.author: Courtney Albon
items.summary: The Space Force may invest in a maneuverable space vehicle that can be available for an on-demand launch in response to “emerging threats,” according to a new industry notice. The post Space Force Seeks Maneuverable Spacecraft for On-Demand Launch appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

The Space Force may invest in a maneuverable space vehicle that can be available for an on-demand launch in response to “emerging threats,” according to a new industry notice.

In a Sept. 18 request for information , Space Systems Command’s Space Safari program office—which leads the service’s Tactically Responsive Space program—said they’re interested in buying a commercial spacecraft that can perform what are known as rendezvous proximity operations and dock to other satellites. The notice specifies a potential need for the capability as soon as fiscal 2029.

“[The] Space Safari program rapidly acquires, integrates, and deployed space systems to address urgent combatant commander needs and emerging threats outside traditional programs of record,” the notice states. “To achieve this, the office seeks innovative, cost-efficient solutions for unpredictable mission requirements.”

The notice doesn’t spell out how many of these vehicles the Space Force might buy but identifies a target “tasking-to-launch” timeline of 14 days. It also stresses the need for modular systems that can integrate a variety of payloads should the service need to swap a system at the last minute.

The Space Force defines Tactically Responsive Space, or TacRS , as the ability to quickly respond to on-orbit threats in any number of ways—from launching a rocket on demand to maneuvering an at-the-ready satellite to replace or augment another to buying commercial space capabilities during a conflict.

Space Safari has been demonstrating and progressing new TacRS capabilities over the last few years. In 2023, Firefly’s Alpha rocket launched a Millennium Space Systems payload just 27 hours after receiving launch orders as part of the service’s Victus Nox mission. Then in late 2025 and early 2026, it conducted a tabletop effort and field exercise called Victus Diem aimed at refining its processes for repeatable rapid launch.

In June, the service launched Victus Haze , which focused on validating multiple TacRS concepts, including dynamic space operations between two satellites. In this case, a Rocket Lab satellite launched on demand and a True Anomaly spacecraft prepositioned on orbit took turns playing the role of adversary and conducting “dynamic engagements” including pursuits between the two satellites.

Those demonstrations have put the service on a path toward operationalizing TacRS concepts. The Space Force’s fiscal 2027 budget request, which includes $86 million for TacRS demonstrations, says Space Safari plans to use funding to support “operational missions requiring both rapid launch and maneuverable, prepositioned capabilities.”

The documents also note that the Space Force plans to establish a “rapid reaction force structure” that would involve having satellites in production and on hand, ready for rapid launch as needed. The Sept. 18 notice appears to be an early step in that direction.

In a briefing at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference, acting portfolio acquisition executive for space combat power Col. Bryon McClain told reporters the service is in the process of transitioning TacRS into an “operational system.” He noted that while the Space Force has additional missions planned, it would likely be saying “less and less” about them.

“You’re probably going to hear a lot less about that overall because we see this as an important warfighting capability, and the last thing you want to do is make that too public,” he said Sept. 16.

For now, the five known TacRS missions expected to launch in the next few years are:

Victus Surgo, a mission cosponsored by the Defense Innovation Unit that will feature a SpaceX Falcon 9 launching a highly maneuverable spacecraft built by Impulse Space

Victus Salo 1, set to launch in 2027 on a Falcon 9 rocket that will carry a payload built by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology

Victus Salo 2 and 3 , which don’t yet have a public timeline but will involve Impulse Space’s pre-positioned Mira orbital maneuver vehicle

Victus Sol, launched by Firefly’s Alpha, which will carry an operational payload

items.title: 8,000 Airmen and Guardians Still Have Medical Shaving Waivers After Policy Changes
items.author: Matthew Cox
items.summary: Around 8,000 Airmen and Guardians currently have medical waivers exempting them from shaving—thousands less than just a few years ago but still about half of all the waivers across the U.S. military. The revelation comes shortly after the Department of the Air Force started directing commanders to consider separating those who have had medical shaving profiles for too long. The post 8,000 Airmen and Guardians Still Have Medical Shaving Waivers After Policy Changes appeared first on <a hre
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

Around 8,000 Airmen and Guardians currently have medical waivers exempting them from shaving—thousands less than just a few years ago but still about half of all the waivers across the U.S. military. The revelation comes shortly after the Department of the Air Force started directing commanders to consider separating those who have had medical shaving profiles for too long.

All of the services are currently refining their policies to align with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s September 2025 mandate that medical shaving waivers be limited to 12 months and those with permanent conditions be evaluated for separation.

Details on the number of waivers have been scarce to this point. But this week, Task & Purpose reported that “as many as 16,300” service members have these waivers. That includes 4,760 Sailors, 3,400 Soldiers, and 144 Marines.

The other 8,000 are Airmen and Guardians, a Department of the Air Force spokesperson confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine. These individuals have “an active temporary medical shaving waiver,” the spokesperson said. They did not immediately provide a breakdown of the waivers between the Air Force and Space Force.

The Air Force currently has about 495,300 Airmen, and the Space Force has roughly 10,400 uniformed Guardians—meaning about 1.6 percent of service members in the department have a waiver.

That’s down significantly from “historical averages” of 18,000 to 20,000 Airmen and 300 Guardians, the department spokesperson said. Military.com has previously reported that the number of medical shaving waivers in the Air Force went from 13,131 to 23,068 between 2021 and 2023.

The department spokesperson noted that the recent drop in waivers was due to “recent policy updates and clinical reevaluations.”

Still, the total number of shaving wavers in the Air Force and Space Force is disproportionally larger than the other services, a reality that could create manning challenges if a large number of those waiver holders wind up being involuntary separated in the future.

The medical shaving waiver total does not include Sikhs, Muslims, and other religious groups who have been permitted to wear beards and other facial hair in uniform under religious accommodations. Hegseth has directed that service members who wear beards under religious accommodations be reevaluated under the pre-2010 appearance standards that generally do not authorize facial hair waivers.

In early August, the DAF directed commanders to begin to consider separating Airmen and Guardians who have held shaving profiles for more than 12 of the past 24 months and who remain unable to conform to grooming standards.

Commanders must either initiate involuntary separation or submit a retention recommendation to their chain of command. Airmen and Guardians separated “solely on the basis of the condition” and not for deliberate disregard of the policy will receive an honorable discharge, the guidance states. Commanders should not use the new policy to separate members who otherwise would be separated for unsatisfactory performance or misconduct, according to the guidance.

In some cases, Airmen and Guardians with medical waivers unable to meet the new facial hair standards could be eligible for retention. Commanders have the option to submit retention recommendations to their chain of command, according to the guidance, which adds that approval could be granted on a “case-by-case” basis if there is a “compelling government interest” for retention, such as:

Low manning and retention rates in the Airman or Guardian’s career specialty

The Airman or Guardian has special experience or specialized training

The cost and time required to replace the individual is extensive

The Airmen or Guardian is close to retirement

Gas Mask Seal Test

In late August, the DAF also released instructions that gives all Airmen and Guardians until Dec. 31 to verify they can achieve a proper protective mask seal, a new requirement Hegseth announced last year as part his crackdown on service members with beards, goatees, and other facial hair.

All Airmen and Guardians must complete a CBRN Defense Foundations Course, an annual web-based course taken through DAF e-Learning. Then they have to achieve a proper protective mask seal by the year-end deadline. The test must be witnessed by a “mask fit validation monitor,” which will be appointed at the Air Force and Space Force squadron level.

Hegseth’s Sept. 30 memo states that “noncompliant personnel—due to refusal, exemption denial, or failed tests—will be flagged as nondeployable in the appropriate Military Service personnel system. Repeated noncompliance may result in administrative separation.”

The CBRN training and mask-seal validation are slated to become annual requirements for Airmen and Guardians.

items.title: Royal Navy successfully launches US Mk 48 torpedo from uncrewed submersible
items.author: Claire Barrett
items.summary: Last week, the Royal Navy successfully launched a U.S.-made Mk 48 Heavyweight Torpedo from a British Excalibur uncrewed underwater vehicle.
items.body:
Naval

Royal Navy successfully launches US Mk 48 torpedo from uncrewed submersible

Sailors aboard the submarine USS California guide a Mk 48 inert training torpedo into place during an expeditionary ordnance loading exercise. (Mass Communication Specialist 1st Class Michael C. Barton/U.S. Navy)

The Royal Navy successfully launched a U.S. Navy Mk 48 Heavyweight Torpedo from a British Excalibur uncrewed underwater vehicle, or UUV, marking a significant step toward allied operational fleets of uncrewed vehicles.

The successful Sept. 13 launch at the British Underwater Test & Evaluation Centre in Scotland highlights a major operational achievement for AUKUS Pillar 2 — a multilateral agreement between the U.S., U.K. and Australia to enable Uncrewed Undersea Vehicle payload systems that can be used across each country’s UUVs, according to the May 2026 agreement .

While still just a proof of concept, the successful test, according to the Navy press release, “validated the mechanical, electrical, and software integration of a U.S. kinetic payload onto an allied autonomous vessel, proving that allied forces can rapidly achieve weapon interchangeability.”

The allied cooperation and testing marks “a historic first for allied undersea warfare,” said Adm. Daryl Caudle, Chief of Naval Operations. “Proving that we can seamlessly launch a U.S. heavyweight torpedo from a Royal Navy autonomous underwater vehicle validates our shared vision for true interchangeability. By integrating weapons, payloads, and mission architectures across allied platforms, we are increasing the flexibility, scale, and combat power of our combined forces and ensuring they are ready to meet the strategic demands of tomorrow.”

The latest version of the Mk 48, the MOD 7, a result of a Joint Development Program with the Royal Australian Navy, is optimized for both “traditional and emerging missions, according to the Navy , while the Excalibur, unveiled in May 2025, is the Royal Navy’s first uncrewed submarine.

From video of the event, it appears that the Mk 48 torpedo was placed under the nearly 40-foot British submersible and launched from a cradle attached to the hull of the UUV.

The Mk 48 torpedo, the U.S. Navy’s standard heavyweight torpedo, stands at 19 feet long with a 21-inch diameter.

According to the U.K.’s Navy Lookout , “Excalibur has no torpedo tubes, but a large central payload bay with doors at the top and bottom. However, the Mk 48 torpedo… is too long to fit in the standard central payload bay.”

With close coordination between the two navies, it is conceivable that future UUVs will deploy sophisticated weapon launch arrangements suitable for both British and American-made technologies.

The successful deployment of the heavyweight torpedo is just the first step under AUKUS Pillar 2.

This proof of concept is just the first step, however, as the U.S. and Royal Navy continue an aggressive “follow-on acceleration with Project CUTLASS” that will utilize the Anduril Dive-XL platform and tackle “advanced payload integration data, command and control architectures, and tactical employment scenarios to further mature uncrewed undersea capabilities,” per the release.

Claire Barrett is an editor and military history correspondent for Military Times. She holds a master's degree in military history from King's College, London, and is also a World War II researcher with an unparalleled affinity for Sir Winston Churchill and Michigan football.

items.title: Jacksonville defense round table links industrial capacity, workforce to military readiness
items.author: Dustin Senger
items.summary: The Marine Corps’ ability to move and sustain forces overseas depends on skilled workers, resilient infrastructure and communities where military families can afford to live, a Marine commander told regional defense leaders Sept. 21 in Jacksonville, Florida.
items.body: JACKSONVILLE, Fla. — The Marine Corps’ ability to move and sustain forces overseas depends on skilled workers, resilient infrastructure and communities where military families can afford to live, a Marine commander told regional defense leaders Sept. 21 in Jacksonville, Florida. U.S. Marine Corps Col. David Merles, commanding officer of Marine Corps Support Facility Blount Island and Blount Island Command, urged Jacksonville and Florida to remain a “beacon for talent” while strengthening the workforce and infrastructure behind the military’s global reach. Merles spoke at the First Coast Defense Round Table, where nearly 60 military, government and industry representatives gathered to discuss defense priorities, infrastructure, workforce development and industrial capacity. The second annual event drew a larger crowd than the inaugural 2025 round table. Participating military organizations included Naval Air Station Jacksonville, Naval Station Mayport, Fleet Readiness Center Southeast, the Florida Air National Guard’s 125th Fighter Wing, U.S. Coast Guard Sector Jacksonville and Naval Submarine Base Kings Bay. Blount Island Command generates, sustains, modernizes and distributes ready-for-issue, service-managed equipment across the Marine Corps’ global positioning network. Marine Corps Support Facility Blount Island provides the industrial infrastructure and maritime access required for that mission. “We’re positioning for advantage, so we can close that force,” Merles said, describing how Marines link with equipment already positioned aboard ships or at ashore sites. He pointed to the facility’s slipway, waterfront infrastructure and rail access, along with neighboring JAXPORT’s commercial Blount Island Marine Terminal, as part of the regional transportation network supporting military power projection. “Everyone on Blount Island, whether on the JAXPORT side or our side, is focused on power projection, enabling our warfighters forward and projecting power from Jacksonville,” Merles said. The Marine Corps mission on the island relies on service members and civilians in operations, logistics, materiel production and naval asset management, with significant support from contractors working under government oversight. “Keep those pipelines open for the workforce,” Merles said. “We need people to get hired and come here and do these great things.” Merles raised cost-of-living concerns for junior Marines and Sailors assigned to the installation. With no barracks or commissary at Marine Corps Support Facility Blount Island, assigned service members rely heavily on the surrounding community for housing and services. “As we continue to grow, and we attract all this talent, and we’re building this maritime industrial base — we’re all-in on that — we’re keeping an eye on the cost of living for our young junior Marines and Sailors,” Merles said. He also called for stronger connections between military sustainment requirements and regional expertise in advanced manufacturing, automation, autonomy and predictive maintenance. Keynote speaker David Norquist, president and CEO of the National Defense Industrial Association and former deputy secretary of defense, reinforced that point. Norquist described Jacksonville as “the epicenter of defense” and framed a strong U.S. defense industrial base as central to deterrence. He identified empowered noncommissioned officers, allies and partners, and industrial innovation as U.S. advantages in strategic competition with China. Washington can set priorities, Norquist said, but communities such as Jacksonville ultimately deliver military capability. He highlighted the region’s veteran workforce and industrial capacity. Harrison Conyers, director of Jacksonville’s Military Affairs and Veterans Department, provided the city’s perspective. He described Jacksonville as striving to remain “the most military-, veteran-friendly community in the United States.” Conyers highlighted the city’s veteran community, its 2026 Great American Defense Community recognition and the Stand for Service Act, which requires companies receiving certain city economic-development incentives to make a good-faith effort to hire qualified veterans and active-duty military spouses for at least 10% of new jobs created through supported projects. “We’re very proud of our military history in Jacksonville, Florida,” Conyers said. Military and defense activity contributes an estimated $9.1 billion to Duval County’s gross regional product and supports more than 68,000 jobs, according to data cited by the City of Jacksonville. U.S. Rep. John Rutherford of Florida then connected federal defense spending to industrial capacity and workforce support. “We have to have a strong industrial base in our country,” Rutherford said. He emphasized workforce development and highlighted funded defense projects in Northeast Florida. “We have to get back to building things in our country.” After the presentations, attendees divided into working groups focused on modernization and infrastructure, workforce development and veteran hiring, and industry alliances and capabilities. The groups identified challenges and developed recommendations for follow-on regional coordination.

items.title: Italian Navy plots race of two local machines: an F-35B against a Ferrari
items.author: Tom Kington
items.summary: The Italian Navy wants to find out if one of its F-35B fighter jets can outrace a Ferrari SF90 on the ground.
items.body:
Europe

Italian Navy plots race of two local machines: an F-35B against a Ferrari

A Lockheed Martin F-35B of the Italian Navy lands at the Los Llanos military base in Albacete, Spain, on Sept. 24, 2025. (Joan Valls/Urbanandsport/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

ROME — The F-35B fighter can take off on a very short runway, hover in the air and land vertically, but the Italian navy is about to find out whether it can also outrace a Ferrari.

In an unusual race planned next month at the Navy’s air base at Grottaglie in southern Italy, one of its F-35Bs will go head-to-head with a Ferrari SF90 to see which has the punchier acceleration.

“We are used to getting a result, but this will be tough,” said Fabio Barone, who will be behind the wheel of the SF90 after claiming seven speed records in a Ferrari.

A Navy spokesman confirmed the race would go ahead.

The first race on Oct. 11 will be over 500 meters on an aluminum runway used by the F-35Bs at Grottaglie for landing. At the end of the course the F-35B will take off.

Barone said the car will normally accelerate from zero to 100 km/h in 2.8 seconds, but with special engine tuning it will do it in 2.6 seconds.

That will allow the car to reach 330 km/h over the 500 meters and complete the course in 8-9 seconds.

“With that acceleration, I will face 2.2g, meaning 140kg of pressure,” he said.

“The F35B will make a slower start but has more power,” he added.

A second race, on asphalt and aluminium, will be run over 2.8 km. After 500 meters the F-35B will take over and complete the race in flight at

an altitude of about 20 metres.

Barone, 54, said the car and the aircraft will race together on one 35 meter wide runway, meaning there will be just 15 meters between them.

“We will be very close,” he said. “The challenge will be driving over the aluminium plates, which will create vibration,” he added.

Asked why exactly he was keen to race against a jet fighter, Barone said, “Everyone can race against another car, and this is a chance to put on a show. Additionally, Michael Schumacher did it,” he said.

In 2003, the former Formula One driver drove a Ferrari Formula One car in races with an Italian Air Force Eurofighter at Italy’s Grosseto air base - an event which drew a crowd of 50,000.

The Eurofighter won 900- and 1,200–meter races without taking off. Schumacher however won a 600-meter race, accelerating from the starting line to reach 294 km/h and complete the course in 9.6 seconds, beating the Eurofighter by two-tenths of a second.

Barone previously worked with the Italian Navy when he drove a Ferrari last year along the flight deck of the Navy’s new Trieste carrier vessel, reaching 164 km/h over about 200 meters before slamming on the brakes to avoid flying off the end of the ship.

Tom Kington is the Italy correspondent for Defense News.

items.title: Navy Aligns Public Works Under Installation Commanding Officers
items.author: Destiny Sibert
items.summary: The Navy today announced the completion of the transfer of public works maintenance teams from Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command (NAVFAC) to Commander, Navy Installations Command (CNIC), placing approximately 10,000 civilian and military personnel under the direct authority of base commanding officers.
items.body:
WASHINGTON (Sept. 22, 2026) – The Navy today announced the completion of the transfer of public works maintenance teams from Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command (NAVFAC) to Commander, Navy Installations Command (CNIC), placing approximately 10,000 civilian and military personnel under the direct authority of base commanding officers.

“This move is all about giving our base commanders the tools and authority they need to get the job done,” said Vice Adm. Scott Gray, Commander, Navy Installations Command. “By putting maintenance teams directly under local command, we can make quicker decisions, prioritize repairs, and keep our bases running smoothly. I am proud to welcome public works professionals to the CNIC team as we work together to support our Sailors, families, and fleet operations.”

The Navy completed the first stage of this realignment in February 2026, transferring approximately 2,000 installation personnel providing facilities management and environmental functions services. The second stage of the realignment completed Sept. 20, 2026, and includes approximately 8,000 installation public works and mission support personnel. The administrative transfer of host nation and U.S. civilian service personnel in Japan will occur Nov. 1, 2026, in accordance with country-specific personnel transfer requirements.

While CNIC will now run everyday base maintenance, NAVFAC will provide infrastructure construction, engineering, and contracting capabilities that enable Navy and Marine Corps lethality.

“NAVFAC and CNIC worked closely together to set the conditions for a seamless transition of public works functions and ensure continuous support to the fleet,” said Rear Adm. Jeff Kilian, Commander, Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command. “This realignment strengthens NAVFAC’s ability to drive acquisition reform and accelerate delivery of infrastructure solutions critical to Navy and Marine Corps warfighting readiness.”

Commander, Navy Installations Command is responsible for worldwide U.S. Navy Shore installation management, designing and developing integrated solutions for sustainment and development of Navy shore infrastructure as well as quality of life programs. CNIC oversees 10 Navy regions, 71 installations, and more than 63,000 employees who are focused on warfighting and manning, training and equipping the Shore to fight and win. Navy installations are warfighting platforms essential to every fleet operation.

items.title: Joint Navy-Marine Corps test advances future fleet anti-submarine capability with MV-22 sonobuoy drops
items.author: Katherine Coughlan
items.summary: A joint test team successfully executed the first lot acceptance test of sonobuoys from an MV-22B Osprey off the coast of San Clemente Island, California Aug. 19.
items.body: A joint test team successfully executed the first lot acceptance test of sonobuoys from an MV-22B Osprey off the coast of San Clemente Island, California Aug. 19. The milestone was conducted by the Air Anti-Submarine Warfare Systems Program Office (PMA-264), the V-22 Joint Program Office (PMA-275), and Marine Operational Test and Evaluation Squadron One (VMX-1). The demonstration validated the tiltrotor aircraft as an alternative platform for the Navy’s sonobuoy quality assurance program (SQAP), boosting operational readiness and laying the groundwork for expanded tactical employment across the fleet. PMA-264 manages SQAP, which subjects random production samples to over-water testing to evaluate reliability and acoustic performance before delivering vendor inventory to operational squadrons. "Our primary focus in the quality assurance program is making sure the sonobuoys delivered to the fleet perform exactly as expected," said Capt. Greg Hinkle, PMA-264 program manager. Historically, the Navy relied on P-3C Orion aircraft assigned to Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 30 (VX-30) to perform quality assurance drops using automated launchers. The test proved the MV-22B Osprey can serve as a dependable substitute if primary test platforms are unavailable, helping prevent testing backlogs and keeping delivery schedules on track. "By utilizing the MV-22 for this type of mission, we are reinforcing our supply chain and ensuring frontline aircrews have the mission-ready stores they need to detect and track undersea threats," Hinkle said. Unlike the P-3, which uses automated launch containers triggered from the cockpit, the MV-22B required aircrew to manually launch the buoys from the open rear cargo ramp. Crew chiefs removed container caps and inverted launch tubes to release the stores into the slipstream. Because manual deployment creates longer gaps between drops than automated launchers, the VMX-1 aircrew adjusted by reducing flight speed, matching the precise target pattern and spacing needed for acoustic testing. "From an aircrew standpoint, this event provided an invaluable opportunity for our pilots and crew chiefs to build proficiency working through the mechanics of manual sonobuoy drops in a controlled setting," said Lt. Col. Brandon Pope, V-22 pilot and VMX-1 advanced projects lead. The hand-launch process requires tight coordination. The pilot holds steady flight parameters while the co-pilot manages navigation, timing, and communications, queuing crew chiefs in the cargo bay to program and release the buoys on schedule. "Hand-launching from an open ramp requires split-second coordination; the crew must be deliberate with timing, airspeed control, and internal communication," Pope said. "This test demonstrated how the V-22’s range, speed, and versatility can support broader maritime domain awareness and distributed fleet operations." In addition to meeting test criteria, the mission also provided operational experience that will help VMX-1 refine tactics, techniques, and procedures for future tiltrotor anti-submarine warfare support. PMA-264 and PMA-275 will analyze acoustic and deployment data from the flights to refine procedures for future quality assurance missions and joint fleet operations.

items.title: CENTCOM has become a battle lab for unmanned systems
items.author: Natalie Oliverio
items.summary: Unmanned systems have moved quickly from experimentation and exercises into the demands of an active war.
items.body:
With the start of operations against Iran, unmanned systems moved from experimentation and exercises into the demands of an active war. Pictured are autonomous surface vessels built by Saronic. (Saronic)

When a U.S. Army helicopter went down near the Strait of Hormuz in June, an unmanned U.S. Navy vessel went looking for the crew.

The Corsair, operated by U.S. 5th Fleet’s Task Force 59 , helped recover two U.S. service members. A month later, three Corsairs were used for something entirely different : striking a submarine and ship maintenance facility at the Bandar Abbas naval base in Iran, marking the “first time American forces have employed sea drones in combat operations,” CENTCOM confirmed .

The two missions illustrate how quickly unmanned systems have moved from experimentation and exercises into the demands of an active war.

A U.S. official told Military Times that American forces are now using unmanned systems “on, above, and below [the sea],” in support of military objectives and said they have been effective, particularly in reducing risk to U.S. forces personnel.

Joshua Tallis, director of Ally and Partner Security Affairs at the Center for Naval Analyses, or CNA, said real-world use of uncrewed systems gives the Navy an “unrivaled opportunity” to learn how to command and deploy robotic systems and refine their deployment, employment and sustainment.

Deployment of unmanned systems

The Navy began Task Force 59 in 2021 to accelerate the integration of unmanned systems and artificial intelligence into operations across the Middle East. The task force used unmanned platforms to expand maritime awareness and work alongside crewed ships and aircraft.

In a 2022 exercise, unmanned vessels identified training targets and relayed information to command centers ashore, while the Navy said the additional sensors could help position crewed ships to respond more rapidly.

By 2024, the service had established Task Group 59.1 to focus on the operational deployment of unmanned systems teamed with manned operators. Task Force 59 personnel participated in more than 30 exercises and operations under its previous commander, according to the Navy.

The Navy’s February 2026 Fighting Instructions lay out specific roles for unmanned platforms. Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle described medium unmanned surface vessels as designed for “scouting, screening, and striking,” while identifying unmanned underwater vehicles for water-space denial, survey and mine warfare. The 2026 guidance also calls for attritable, easily replenishable unmanned surface vessels as part of the fleet’s force design.

That Navy effort is now unfolding alongside a separate CENTCOM push to put unmanned systems directly into combat.

CENTCOM has already begun building a combat-focused unmanned force. In December 2025, the command established Task Force Scorpion Strike as the military’s first dedicated one-way attack drone squadron in the Middle East.

The task force employed low-cost one-way attack drones during Operation Epic Fury . At the same time, CENTCOM used unmanned attack vessels during the July strikes on Iranian port facilities, according to the command.

In August, CENTCOM announced plans for Task Force Falcon Strike , a multinational, multidomain attack-drone task force that will use one-way attack drones from above, on and below the sea. CENTCOM said Falcon Strike would expand attack-drone capabilities across the Middle East with regional partners.

The Fighting Instructions also envision unmanned and manned units operating with varying degrees of independence. Caudle said the Navy will use “Delegated Autonomy Levels” to define “what a unit manned or unmanned can do independently,” based in part on its ability to sense the battlespace, synthesize what matters and deliver effects without waiting for higher headquarters.

Combat risks

Combat puts additional demands on unmanned systems, including maintaining communications, operating for extended periods, navigating contested waters and remaining useful when an adversary is actively trying to interfere with them.

The systems are no longer being judged only in an exercise environment. They are being judged in real time by what happens when an adversary is working to stop them.

Despite the opportunities provided by deploying uncrewed systems in the current conflict, Tallis cautioned against drawing broad conclusions from it. The public examples from the war, he said, should be viewed as “an iterative learning moment, not a fully formed vision of the future fight.”

Cost is one unresolved issue. Open-source estimates put a Corsair at about $1.1 million, Tallis said. That raises a broader question about what it means for an unmanned system to be considered “attritable,” “consumable” or “expendable.”

The war has also exposed the risks that come with putting unmanned systems into contested waters.

In September, Iran said it had captured an Anduril Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicle that had malfunctioned while surveying regional waters. CENTCOM said the vehicle was an older model that did not collect sensitive data or carry classified sonar or radar equipment.

More recently, CENTCOM said two Iranian boats attempted to take possession of a U.S. Saildrone unmanned surface vessel operating in the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. forces destroyed the boats, according to the command.

According to Tallis, there is an unanswered question of how much risk the military should accept when deploying uncrewed systems, including how to determine when a system has delivered enough value to justify its loss. Many unmanned systems are cheaper than crewed platforms, he said, but “not, per se, cheap.”

Tallis said unmanned systems remain particularly well suited to surveillance, consistent with their use by the U.S. over the past two decades. But there is not yet enough evidence to demonstrate a meaningful change in the use of unmanned surface vessels for strike.

Search-and-rescue missions could also require platforms to be positioned across a theater to provide quick reaction times, something Tallis said does not yet appear to be widely fielded.

Natalie Oliverio is an independent journalist and Navy veteran who covers military and veterans’ issues. Drawing on her experience as a talent executive and mentor, she writes about the policies, people and programs shaping the military community.

items.summary: An F-16 fighter jet assigned to the US air base Spangdahlem in western Germany crashed on Tuesday, according to U.S. officials.
items.body:
Air Warfare

F-16 fighter jet crashes at US air base in western Germany

The F-16 is a multi-role fighter aircraft capable of both air-to-air and air-to-ground combat. (Staff Sgt. Steven Cardo/Air Force)

An F-16 fighter jet assigned to the US air base Spangdahlem in western Germany crashed on Tuesday, the U.S. military said, adding that one pilot had ejected safely and was receiving medical treatment.

The cause of the incident is under investigation, the military said in a statement, with emergency response personnel at the scene of the crash.

Germany’s air traffic control authority, in a separate statement, said a total of four F-16s had been taking part in a training exercise.

“Two were still in the training area, while two were returning to Spangdahlem Air Base. One of these two jets is believed to have crashed while on approach,” it said, adding the remaining F-16s had landed at the US Air Force base in Ramstein.

items.title: F-16 Crashes in Germany; Pilot Successfully Ejects
items.author: Chris Gordon
items.summary: A U.S. Air Force F-16 Fighting Falcon crashed on a local mission in Germany on Sept. 22. The pilot ejected safely and is receiving medical care, Air Force officials said. The fighter was assigned to the 52nd Fighter Wing at Spangdahlem Air Base. The jet went down on base property in the Eifel region of western Germany. The post F-16 Crashes in Germany; Pilot Successfully Ejects appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

A U.S. Air Force F-16 Fighting Falcon crashed on a local mission in Germany on Sept. 22.

The pilot ejected safely and received medical care, Air Force officials said. The fighter was assigned to the 52nd Fighter Wing at Spangdahlem Air Base.

In a statement, the wing said the jet was returning to base after a four-ship “routine training flight” when it crashed on approach to Spangdahlem’s sole runway around 2:30 p.m. local time. The incident occurred on base property near the runway. The three other F-16s diverted to Ramstein Air Base, Germany, and landed safely. Air Force officials did not provide further details on the extent of the pilot’s injuries.

The wing said that the cause of the crash is under investigation. Air Force emergency personnel and local German rescue crews responded to the incident.

This is the second F-16 crash for the Air Force in five days—a Viper belonging to the Texas Air National Guard’s 149th Fighter Wing crashed during a training mission in Michigan on Sept. 17. The pilot in that crash ejected safely as well.

The 52nd Fighter Wing has one squadron of F-16s that specializes in the “Wild Weasel” mission of suppressing enemy air defenses. The U.S. military deployed fighters from the unit to the Middle East twice during the seven-month conflict with Iran. Forward deployments typically consist of a dozen fighter jets, and Spangdahlem has over two dozen F-16s that comprise the 52nd Fighter Wing’s sole fighter squadron, the 480th Fighter Squadron. The 480th is permanently based at Spangdahlem as part of U.S. Air Forces in Europe.

Images posted to social media and captured by local press show a charred hunk of the F-16, including what appears to be its engine, amid a wide debris field. Black smoke billowed over the base as emergency personnel responded to the scene.

items.title: South Korea faces no good choices in sending forces for Trump’s unpopular Iran mission
items.author: Leilani Chavez
items.summary: Experts worry that U.S. requests for troop contributions to America's faraway campaigns could leave South Korea exposed when it matters most.
items.body:
Asia Pacific

South Korea faces no good choices in sending forces for Trump’s unpopular Iran mission

South Korean sailors salute during a ceremony marking the launch of the "Cheonghae" unit. (Choi Jae-Ho/AFP via Getty Images)

MANILA, Philippines — As Washington presses South Korea to contribute to securing the Strait of Hormuz, experts said Seoul is facing a military capacity dilemma , as forces could get stretched amid escalating threats from North Korea.

The worry comes as Washington exerts pressure on South Korea to support U.S. operations in the Strait of Hormuz , where the war with Iran is choking worldwide oil supplies, even while North Korean threats escalate.

The South Korean Army reported that the North had fired two ballistic missiles on Sunday and earlier this month launched a 5,000-ton guided missile destroyer in the Pacific.

The security environment in East Asia raises a military allocation concern, especially since South Korean officials mentioned sending a “practical contribution” to U.S. efforts in the Middle East.

“If such [U.S.] requests become recurrent, Seoul could face trade-offs between extra-regional missions and deterrence around the Korean Peninsula,” Ju Hyung Kim, president of Security Management Institute, a Seoul-based defense think tank, told Defense News.

Last week, President Lee Jae Myeong had drawn the line and said there would be “no deployment to a war.”

The government may instead extend the activities of the Cheonghae Unit, a naval task force group stationed in the Sea of Aden for counter-piracy operations.

The Cheonghae Unit is a small maritime task group that includes a KDX-II destroyer, a maritime helicopter, as well as Marines, naval special forces and support personnel.

The Cheonghae may be the “least burdensome option,” Kim said, and would allow the Lee government to skirt the domestic political costs of a troop deployment and provide a military contribution.

While the range of operations could extend from Somalia to the Middle East, an expert based in Seoul told Defense News on condition of anonymity that the unit’s role will be limited to protecting South Korean ships and conducting humanitarian assistance activities.

“I don’t see the possibility of upgrade or recalibration … given the current security situation in the region,” the expert said.

Either way, the Cheonghae detachment would be navigating rough waters. Esmaeil Baqaei, spokesperson for Iran’s Foreign Ministry, warned on Sept. 7 that any foreign military involvement in the strait could face serious consequences.

Iranian academic Mohammad Marandi said that Tehran could regard South Korea as an enemy and target Korean economic and military assets across the Persian Gulf if Seoul joined a U.S.-led effort to secure the Strait of Hormuz.

The warnings had escalated anxieties in Seoul, where the deployment question remains a point of contention.

If South Korean personnel or assets are targeted, Lee would be pressured to either “escalate by deploying combat forces or to scale back to contain domestic backlash and protect his political standing,” Kim said.

“Seoul would need to define the mission, geographical scope, rules of engagement and command arrangements very carefully, while also managing external expectations about what a ‘practical contribution’ actually entails,” Kim said.

The government had begun to assess contribution requirements, which experts said are evident in an earlier recon mission to the United Arab Emirates to examine the Al Dhafra Air Base and Jebel Ali Port.

Findings from the trip have not been made public. But a successive mission to Bahrain, which hosts the U.S. Fifth Fleet, U.S. Naval Forces Central Command and the multinational Combined Maritime Forces, “could involve examining basing, logistics, intelligence-sharing, maritime-domain awareness and coordination with multinational forces,” Kim said.

The Cheonghae Unit may be enough to appease Washington for now, especially after Seoul committed a $20 billion investment in an energy project in Texas, Kim said.

But the larger challenge is the precedent it might create: President Donald Trump might expect additional contributions as the conflict in the Middle East continues.

And Kim said force allocation will become a graver concern if alliance commitments take South Korean assets far from the peninsula for a prolonged period of time.

“A P-8A deployed to the Gulf, for example, cannot simultaneously perform maritime-surveillance or anti- submarine missions around the Korean Peninsula,” he said.

“So the key question is not simply whether the Cheonghae Unit is sufficient now, but whether it becomes the beginning of recurring U.S. expectations for South Korean deployments beyond Northeast Asia,” Kim said.

Leilani Chavez is an Asia correspondent for Defense News. Her reporting expertise is in East Asian politics, development projects, environmental issues and security.

items.title: US Army awards Lockheed Martin $1.2B PrSM contract
items.author: Michael Peck
items.summary: The U.S. Army awarded Lockheed Martin a PrSM contract worth up to $1.2 billion.
items.body:
Industry

US Army awards Lockheed Martin $1.2B PrSM contract

The Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) was recently fired from a U.S. Army M270A2 and HIMARS at White Sands Missile Range, New Mexico. (Christopher Bohn/U.S. Army)

The U.S. Army awarded Lockheed Martin a $1.2 billion contract for its short-range ballistic missiles.

The indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity contract covers initial production and future orders of Increment 2 of the Precision Strike Missile, or PrSM , according to a Lockheed Martin announcement .

“This award marks an important step in delivering PrSM Increment 2 to the warfighter,” Dave Griser, Lockheed Martin vice president for precision fires, said in the announcement. “We’re ready to move from flight testing into production and provide the Army with an expanded long-range precision fires capability.”

PrSM is intended to replace the Army Tactical Missile System, first fielded in the early 1990s. It has a range of about 500 kilometers, versus about 300 kilometers for the ATACMS. PrSM can be launched from the M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket System and the M270 Multiple Launch Rocket System.

PrSM Increment 2 features a multimode seeker that can lock on to moving targets on land. It can also hit ships moving at sea, giving land-based launchers a maritime strike capability.

Lockheed Martin is currently conducting flight testing of the new PrSM version.

“PrSM Increment 2 completed its first flight test in March and its second flight test in August — obtaining critical data during flight, launching from a HIMARS, deploying protective covers and engaging the target,” the manufacturer said.

More PrSM Increment 2 flight tests are scheduled for 2027.

PrSM recently made its controversial combat debut in the Iran war. Analysts believe a PrSM missile, which sprays a cloud of pellets, killed dozens of civilians in the Iranian city of Lamerd on Feb. 28, the first day of U.S.-Israeli strikes against Iran. U.S. Central Command has denied the accusation.

The U.S. military faces a desperate shortage of strike and air defense missiles after expending vast numbers in Iran. This reportedly includes a lack of PrSM weapons.

The new contract builds on the Department of Defense’s broader investment in ballistic missiles, according to Lockheed Martin.

“Lockheed Martin is expanding capacity to quadruple PrSM production while continuing to develop additional PrSM increments,” the company said.

Michael Peck is a correspondent for Defense News and a columnist for the Center for European Policy Analysis. He holds an M.A. in political science from Rutgers University. Find him at theuncommondefense.com. His email is mikedefense1@gmail.com.

items.title: Netanyahu May Have Ignored a Dire Warning. Israel Ignores the Deeper Threat.
items.summary: Israel's strategy in Gaza is only keeping Hamas in power: deterred, but not replaced, with no real alternative given a chance. A different outcome calls for a different approach.
items.body:
Commentary

Sep 22, 2026

Displaced Palestinians shelter near a damaged tower in Gaza City, September 20, 2026

By Shira Efron

This commentary was originally published by The Hill on September 22, 2026.

Israelis are still debating whether the recent report is true—whether the United Arab Emirates warned Israel of an imminent Hamas attack roughly 10 days before the Oct. 7 massacre.

But fixating on the few days before Oct. 7 obscures a deeper flaw: The Israeli mindset, the strategic conception , remains largely unchanged. It is conflict management. Israel is using a weakened and deterred Hamas ruling Gaza as an excuse to deepen the divide between Gaza and a Palestinian Authority–run West Bank. By avoiding allowing any alternative to emerge, it is sidelining the Palestinian question altogether.

If the deadliest disaster of Jews since the Holocaust should have changed one thing, it was this. Yet, strip away the rhetoric of “ total victory ,” and Israel’s Gaza policy today looks quite similar, just with more bloodshed and rubble.

In recent weeks, Israeli leaders have vowed to remain in Gaza for the long term and end Hamas’s rule once and for all. Following a string of successful assassinations of Hamas commanders, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz declared : “Our message is clear: No terrorist is immune, and Hamas will not be in Gaza.”

Israel is using a weakened and deterred Hamas ruling Gaza as an excuse to deepen the divide between Gaza and a Palestinian Authority–run West Bank.

Weakening Hamas is legitimate, and so is Israel’s demand that it relinquish control of Gaza. But Israel’s revealed preference tells a different story.

Even as Israel holds an estimated 60 percent of Gaza , Hamas still controls over 95 percent of the population. Hamas is both a terrorist organization and Gaza’s de facto government; removing the former requires an alternative for the latter. Israel refused to hand that role to the Palestinian Authority but signed on to President Trump’s 20-point plan last year, which offers exactly that: a transition to the technocratic National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, eventually leading to a reformed Palestinian Authority.

The Israeli government apparently never intended to let that alternative emerge.

Members of the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza remain in Cairo, with no timeline for entering Gaza. Roughly 6,000 vetted police recruits, meant to begin training months ago, have not left Gaza because Israel will not commit to letting them return.

Construction of a base for the International Stabilization Force is stalled by bureaucracy. Reconstruction of the Israeli-held “Green Zone” meant to showcase non-Hamas governance hasn’t advanced. And in the West Bank, Israeli policy is weakening the Palestinian Authority toward collapse and carving the territory into cantons to ensure no Palestinian governance, with or without Gaza, is ever viable.

Hamas has expectedly stalled the plan, too. But in August it accepted the Board of Peace’s roadmap, listing 15 principles for phased disarmament in exchange for Israel Defense Forces withdrawal. Israel has valid concerns, including the roadmap’s timeline, scope of disarmament, and Qatar and Turkey’s role in verifying compliance.

A future Israeli government that wants a different outcome will have to act like it.

But justified skepticism does not excuse refusing to engage. Instead of making Hamas back its words, Israel has effectively handed it veto power over the process, drawing international blame for stalling while Hamas gains recognition as a legitimate partner.

Domestic politics explains much of this. Israel faces a charged election on Oct. 27 , and Netanyahu’s coalition cannot show compromise on Gaza. Even pressure from Trump plays in his favor, as he claims to be the only one who can stand up to who he called “the greatest friend that the state of Israel has ever had in the White House.” Netanyahu’s rivals, meantime, are trying to outflank him from the right, vowing to keep fighting rather than engage the U.S.-led plan.

But whoever wins will still have to pick up the Trump framework. The alternatives—renewed full-scale war or a Gaza permanently split between an Israeli-held east and Hamas-run west—serve neither Israel’s security interests nor produce an acceptable status quo.

Rather than campaigning on the same hawkish instinct, prime minister contenders should say that the current approach only keeps Hamas in power: deterred, but not replaced, with no real alternative given a chance.

A future Israeli government that wants a different outcome will have to act like it. This means setting a political horizon instead of managing the conflict incident by incident, taking initiative on the Trump plan and disarmament roadmap instead of being dragged along by Washington, Cairo, or Doha.

It also requires letting the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza function and supporting Palestinian Authority reform rather than treating its flaws as a pretext for exclusion and redirecting Gaza’s financial lifelines to starve Hamas economically rather than merely bombing it.

Such a shift could unlock the funding, troops, and regional cooperation the plan needs, and begin restoring Israel’s ties with Europe and the Arab world.

A new government will find it hard to change course quickly. The only way to make that happen is U.S. leadership from the top, because whoever wins will want Trump on their side.

The ceasefire, the hostages’ return, and the 20-point framework a year ago were a major achievement. The Trump administration can use this anniversary and Israel’s election to press ahead. Otherwise, Israel risks drifting back into an Oct. 6 reality: a contained, managed Hamas quietly rebuilding behind a calm facade, primed to explode again.

items.title: US to open two new military bases in Greenland, sources say
items.author: Stine Jacobsen, Erin Banco and Gram Slattery, Reuters
items.summary: The U.S. plans to re-establish a Cold War-era military base in southern Greenland and set up another on the east coast, according to sources.
items.body:
Europe

US to open two new military bases in Greenland, sources say

U.S. Vice President JD Vance tours the U.S. military's Pituffik Space Base in Greenland on March 28, 2025. (Jim Watson/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

COPENHAGEN/WASHINGTON — The U.S. plans to re-establish a Cold War-era military base in southern Greenland and set up another on the east coast, now used by the Danish dog sled patrol, under a deal to be signed with Denmark and Greenland on Tuesday, according to three people familiar with the matter.

The sites are Narsarsuaq, whose population has dwindled to a few dozen people since the U.S. closed its Bluie West One military base in the 1950s, and Mestersvig, a military outpost used by the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, a Danish special forces unit, said two of the people.

Denmark, Greenland and the United States are expected to sign their new agreement at the United Nations General Assembly in New York City at 10:30 a.m. ET (1430 GMT) on Tuesday.

The text of the agreement has not been made public and the three people familiar with the deal, speaking on condition of anonymity, said its details will not be finalized until it is signed.

The governments of Denmark and Greenland did not immediately respond to a request by Reuters for comment.

A White House spokesperson declined to comment on the details of the agreement, repeating an earlier statement that its signing on Tuesday would “secure and defend the security of Greenland and the United States.”

Denmark says the agreement puts Arctic security under the watch of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, the military defense alliance, rather than leaving it solely to the U.S. and Denmark.

The deal follows months of pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump, who has long said he wants the U.S. to control Greenland and has at times refused to rule out military or economic force to acquire the semi-autonomous Danish territory. The idea has been rejected by an overwhelming majority of Greenlanders, polling shows.

Trump’s threats, which peaked in January, triggered a diplomatic crisis within NATO and pushed Denmark and Greenland into negotiations with Washington aimed at defusing the pressure.

During the Cold War, the US maintained 17 military installations and more than 10,000 personnel in Greenland. Today only Pituffik Space Base remains, with some 150 U.S. military personnel.

items.title: The Golden Dome czar must get control of all US missile defense programs
items.author: Thane Clare
items.summary: The Defense Department must heed a vital organizational lesson from the past if Golden Dome is to succeed, writes analyst Thane Clare.
items.body:
Opinion

The Golden Dome czar must get control of all US missile defense programs

U.S. President Donald Trump during an announcement of plans for the Golden Dome defense system in the Oval Office of the White House on May 20, 2025. (Demetrius Freeman/The Washington Post via Getty Images)

The United States is largely defenseless against Russian and Chinese aerial attacks. This is a major strategic problem in today’s era of massed drone and missile warfare—and no one is clearly in charge of solving it.

President Trump’s February 2025 executive order, “The Iron Dome for America” (later rebranded as Golden Dome ), directed the Department of Defense to protect U.S. citizens and infrastructure from all forms of aerial attack. The department took a first step toward assigning responsibility for a U.S. air and missile defense architecture by standing up the Golden Dome office. But critical elements of any near-term defensive shield remain outside its control: namely, the U.S. air and missile defense systems that have proven their worth on Ukrainian and Middle Eastern battlefields.

The Aegis system, for example, is a U.S. Navy program—though its ballistic missile defense component is funded by the Missile Defense Agency (MDA). Patriot interceptors, in turn, belong to the Army . Theater High Altitude Aerial Defense (THAAD) batteries and the Ground Based Midcourse Defense System (GMDS) are developed by the MDA but operated and maintained by the Army. U.S. Northern Command is responsible for U.S. air surveillance but relies heavily on radars belonging to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) — and so on.

RELATED

Iran war has cost $38 billion, depleted two-thirds of US missile interceptors, CBO says

The U.S. military has incurred about $38 billion in costs from combat operations against Iran, a new Congressional Budget Office analysis found.

The Golden Dome director’s position in the Defense Department hierarchy — reporting directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense — reflects the urgency of the task. But it does not convey any actual authority to direct the decisions of the Army, Navy, Air Force, or Transportation secretaries.

Diffusion of responsibility is a recipe for failure.

For Golden Dome to work, the Defense Department must draw on lessons from some of its most successful Cold War innovations — specifically, the organizational innovations that made its game-changing technologies and operational concepts possible. Admiral Hyman Rickover, perhaps the leading exemplar of Cold War innovation, took nuclear propulsion from the blackboard to the fleet in just five years.

To quote Rickover: “Unless you can point your finger at the one person who is responsible when something goes wrong, then you have never had anyone really responsible.” Golden Dome fails this test, precisely because — according to the Defense Department itself — it is a “team effort” in which “we’re going to need all the services and agencies that do this kind of work to step up.”

Rickover took the opposite approach. If something was critical to the Navy’s nuclear propulsion program, he established de facto (and often de jure) control over it. For example, he successfully co-opted the Cabinet-level Atomic Energy Commission. Established in 1947 to oversee all U.S. nuclear matters, the AEC was a potential bureaucratic roadblock. At Rickover’s prompting, therefore, the Navy issued him orders to “report for duty with the Division of Reactor Development” in the AEC (and to the Navy for “additional duty”).

With one foot in the Navy and the other in the AEC, Rickover became the central U.S. authority for nuclear propulsion. This allowed him to coordinate the activities of two separate executive departments, often by proposing an action from one department and then convincing the other to approve it. His dual office, Naval Reactors, remains part of both the Navy and the Department of Energy (successor to the AEC) to this day.

The Rickover approach is not how the Pentagon normally does business. “I can assure you,” Rickover told Congress in 1979, “that having one individual responsible for a total program is a unique concept within the Department of Defense.” But Rickover made it his business to acquire unchallenged authority over all areas that concerned “his” reactors.

The Secretary of Defense must likewise assign total responsibility for Golden Dome, with autonomy and authority to match. This will entail taking the requisite authorities from their normal stewards and re-delegating them to the Golden Dome director.

For example, ballistic missile defense responsibility is currently bifurcated between Golden Dome and the Missile Defense Agency. MDA should be moved under Golden Dome. Similarly, airspace surveillance operations and modernization are divided between DoD and the FAA, with the latter contributing the lion’s share. The Golden Dome director must have a Rickover-like dual assignment in the FAA. And if homeland defense is indeed an urgent priority, DoD should take a hard look at whether the Aegis and Patriot programs should be moved under Golden Dome as well.

This process will be challenging, but far from impossible. And while Rickover’s nuclear power program is one of the most remarkable Cold War innovations, other success stories such as General Bernard Schriever’s Atlas ICBM and Undersecretary of Defense William Perry’s F-117 stealth fighter applied the same core insight: comprehensive organizational authority is just as important as any technological or industrial-base factor. DoD must heed this lesson if Golden Dome is to succeed.

Thane Clare is a Senior Fellow at the Center for Strategic and Budgetary Assessments.

items.title: UK military support to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia
items.summary: The UK will provide additional defensive military support to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia following renewed Houthi attacks and escalating violence in the region.
items.body:
The UK will provide additional defensive military support to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia following renewed Houthi attacks and escalating violence in the region.

Following a request from the Saudi Arabian Government, the UK has agreed to provide an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft to support Saudi defensive activity in support of the legitimate government of Yemen.

Escalating tensions in the Gulf can have a serious impact at home in the UK – increasing prices, disruption to energy supplies, and extra costs for British businesses. The Houthis are a dangerous threat to regional stability in the Middle East, and it is in the UK’s national economic and security interest that they do not succeed.

We unequivocally condemn the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and are clear that the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen have the right to defend themselves.

The support builds on the UK’s existing military contribution to Saudi Arabia’s air defence, including the deployment of air defence equipment and UK personnel helping to protect against missile and drone attacks.

Saudi Arabia and Yemen are long-standing partners of the United Kingdom and play a vital role in regional stability. It is in the UK’s interest to protect regional stability, protecting vital trade and energy supplies and encouraging a diplomatic resolution to the conflict in Yemen.

items.title: Air Force to Get First Next-Gen Tactical C2 Centers By Year’s End
items.author: Todd South
items.summary: A single-pallet-sized tactical operations center is slated to begin shipping to 70 Air Force units by the end of the year following a recent announcement by the company that made it and the Air Force entity responsible for its development. The post Air Force to Get First Next-Gen Tactical C2 Centers By Year’s End appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —The first of 70 single-pallet-sized tactical operations centers are slated to begin shipping to Air Force units by the end of the year following a recent announcement by the company that made it and the Air Force entity responsible for its development.

The Tactical Operations Center-Light is the Air Force’s next-generation method for conducting ground-based air battle management Several years ago, the service contracted with Lockheed Martin and L3Harris to build the first 16 prototypes of the TOC-L, which started delivering in 2023.

In 2025, though, the Air Force tapped Booz Allen Hamilton for a $315 million rapid prototyping contract to scale and produce the second iteration of the TOC-L, dubbed MR2 for Major Release 2 or Material Release 2.

The initial 16 MR1 prototypes let Airmen to get their hands on a prototype system and test it out. MR2 is the kit that will be in place to run air battle management in the near term.

“Material Release 1 is, ‘hey, how do we get the capability they need now so they can fight tonight?” Brig. Gen. Joshua Williams, program acquisition executive for command, control, communications, and battle management, told reporters Sept. 16 at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference. “Material Release 2 is focused on deeper integration, improved edge connectivity, and more mature support.”

The system connects to all major aircraft and capabilities the Air Force deploys and can work backward-compatible through the DAF Battle Network, Patrick Hamilton, vice president for defense technology at Booz, told Air & Space Forces Magazine at the conference.

“This is the next-generation C2 system that the Air Force is going to deploy that hopefully will be in place for the next 30 to 40 years for the new C2 fight,” Hamilton said.

Because the TOC-L system can incorporate software changes more readily than legacy ground systems such as the Control and Reporting Center, it can more quickly add in capabilities, applications, and other items from the DAF Battle Network as it grows and more options are added.

“That is the fundamental difference to the prior prototype,” Hamilton said. “Now you’ll be able to, in the future, iterate as future improvements go online in the Battle Network.”

Operational Air Force units have spent the past year taking and testing TOC-L systems “downrange,” Col. Bai Lan Zhu, senior materiel leader for the Advanced Battle Management System, told reporters during the conference media session.

The total number of TOC-Ls to flow across the entire Air Force is still evolving, Zhu said.

“The exact quantities are something that the operational community is going to refine over time,” she said.

The first wave of TOC-Ls will begin shipping to units by or before December. The company plans to deliver 70 units under the current contract, Hamilton said.

The new system can also draw from at least three “enclaves” of data, letting users fuse information from both classified and unclassified sources more easily.

“So, if you have something coming in, let’s say from an FAA unclassified radar, and you want to put that on the situational awareness [common operating picture] that the user is looking at, which is in a secret enclave, you need the ability to move that data up,” Hamilton said.

The TOC-L provides that ability.

The system can also render those enclaves unclassified when powered off, based on National Security Agency data-at-rest standards.

In the past, system users would spend hours at the end of each mission or shift physically removing a series of drives, labeling them and storing them according to protocols, only to have to rebuild the setup the next day, Mike Lewis, Booz’s chief engineer for TOC-L, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.

“There are a lot of logistics and risk in that type of scenario, so with data at rest being unclassified, it’s a real key to making this tactically relevant from a speed perspective and from a cyber perspective,” Lewis said.

Fewer Pieces, Fewer People

TOC-L replaces the Cold War-era Control and Reporting Center, previously centered around the trusty but bulky AN/TPS-75 radar system.

The legacy system required as many as six C-17 Globemaster IIIs to transport all of its components, using radar dishes, heavy vehicles, and nearly two dozen power generators.

The CRC would require hundreds of Airmen to set up and operate and could take between 24 and 72 hours to set up and tear down.

TOC-L is a feather by comparison.

It fits on a single pallet, with one additional pallet to hold its generator; can be transported inside a single C-130 Hercules; requires about 10 Airmen to operate; and can be set up or torn down in less than an hour.

The TOC-L can squeeze into such a small frame and use far fewer people, partly because of advances in electronics and partly because it can tap into the DAF Battle Network and other networks to access radar and other feeds instead of carrying its own radars into the fight.

The shift in allowing nonproprietary equipment to hook into the TOC-L system also drastically trims down the amount of hardware needed to operate the system’s crucial functions, Hamilton told Air & Space Forces Magazine.

“We’re going to collect iterative feedback from ABMS and the user community as it deploys all over the world,” said Hamilton. “And I think over the next 12 to 24 months, that will start to define what [Material Release 3] will look like and what we hear from the user community, what they prioritize for.”
