items.title: Guidance: MAA Recognition
items.summary: Recognition is the process used to evaluate other military aviation regulators and assess the potential to use their airworthiness outputs within MAA processes.
items.body:
The Recognition process provides a structured evidence base to support a judgement on the extent to which another military aviation regulator’s technical airworthiness outputs would be acceptable for use within the MAA Certification or Organisational Approvals processes.

Recognition, however, does not mean that the work of another military aviation regulator can be used in the UK’s Defence Air Environment without further analysis. Their work must still be understood and assessed by the relevant DE&S Delivery Team Type Airworthiness Authority, in consultation with the MAA , with any differences that present a risk identified and sentenced. Further information about the use of Recognition within MAA processes can be found in Regulatory Articles 1005 and 5810 .

Further details

To undertake Recognition with other military aviation regulators the MAA uses the European Military Airworthiness Document Recognition ( EMAD R ) process developed through the European Defence Agency ( EDA ). This process revolves around the analysis of the other military regulator’s Responses to the Military Authorities’ Recognition Questionset ( MARQ ). The MARQ is contained in Annex D of the EMAD R and is derived from the International Civil Aviation Organization’s Doc 9734 (Safety Oversight Manual) and Doc 9760 (Airworthiness Manual).

The EMAD R can be found on the EDA airworthiness webpage

Evaluation of the Responses to the MARQ enables the MAA to assess the scope of another military aviation regulator’s responsibilities and regulations in the following areas:

general functions of an airworthiness authority

airworthiness inspection regulations

production oversight regulations

aircraft certification regulations

Military aviation regulators can decide to conduct Recognition on a one-way or a two-way (ie mutual) basis, depending on the business need of the nations involved.

The EMAD R process is being used widely by military aviation regulators and it is also the basis for the Five Eyes Air Force Interoperability Council Recognition process and the NATO Recognition Process.

For further information please contact the MAA ’s International Engagement and Recognition Team via:

Email: DSA- MAA -MRPEnquiries@mod.gov.uk

items.title: Latvia chooses Czech howitzers over Swedish Archer offer
items.author: Jaroslaw Adamowski
items.summary: Latvia will buy Czech Morana 155 mm howitzers, reversing an earlier decision to by the rival Archer artillery weapon from Sweden's BAE Systems Bofors.
items.body:
Europe

Latvia chooses Czech howitzers over Swedish Archer offer

The Morana self-propelled howitzer, made by Excalibur Army, a subsidiary of Czechoslovak Group. (Excalibur Army)

WARSAW, Poland — Latvia’s government has approved the acquisition of Morana 155 mm self-propelled wheeled howitzers from Czech manufacturer Excalibur Army, reversing its earlier decision to pursue a deal with Sweden’s BAE Systems Bofors, the producer of the rival Archer artillery system.

“The decision was made following an assessment of the costs of the offers, delivery times, operational capabilities and the involvement of the local defense industry in the procurement,” the Latvian Ministry of Defence said in a statement.

In June 2025, Latvia and Sweden signed a letter of intent that was to pave the way for an acquisition of 18 Archer systems. However, Riga’s decision to continue its negotiations with Excalibur Army resulted in an offer that includes more favorable prices and delivery terms, according to the ministry.

“Another significant advantage is that the involvement of the local defense industry is envisaged as part of the contract,” the statement said.

Bolstering Latvian indirect fire support capabilities has been identified as one of the “key capability development projects” to be financed by the nation’s record-high 2026 defense budget. This year, Latvia foresees spending 4.91% of its gross domestic product (GDP), or €2.16 billion ($2.48 billion), on the military.

The value of the howitzer procurement was not disclosed.

Excalibur Army is a subsidiary of Czechoslovak Group (CSG), the Prague-based private defense holding that is one of Europe’s largest ammunition producers.

The Morana has a firing range of 41.5 km (26 miles). Operated by a crew of three, the howitzer can reach a top road speed of 90 km/h (56 mph), according to data from Excalibur Army.

“The crew has 45 carried rounds available for their task completion. Fully automated gun loading allows the crew to fire up to 6 rounds within the first minute from establishing position,” CSG said in a statement.

Jaroslaw Adamowski is the Poland correspondent for Defense News.

items.title: Housing reforms give military families greater say over their homes
items.summary: Military families will have a greater say over the homes they live in under a package of reforms designed to cut bureaucracy, strengthen accountability and put residents at the heart of housing services.
items.body:
A new Red Tape Challenge, announced today by the Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, will invite military families to identify and remove outdated housing rules, while new national and regional committees will ensure their experiences directly influence future decisions about accommodation services and a ground-breaking pilot will give them a role in signing off repairs to their homes.

The measures build on recent changes already introduced by the Ministry of Defence, including ending outdated restrictions on keeping pets and giving families greater freedom to decorate their homes.

They form part of the Government’s £9.2 billion Defence Housing Strategy, which will transform military housing through the new Defence Housing Service, delivering better homes, improved service standards and a stronger focus on the needs of Service personnel and their families.

Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting MP, said:

Service families should not feel that decisions about their homes are being made without them. These reforms are about giving families more power and control, with a stronger voice in shaping housing services and a clear route to challenge things that aren’t working. Alongside major investment in defence housing, we are determined to build a service that listens and delivers the standard of housing our Armed Forces and their families deserve.

Service families should not feel that decisions about their homes are being made without them. These reforms are about giving families more power and control, with a stronger voice in shaping housing services and a clear route to challenge things that aren’t working.

Alongside major investment in defence housing, we are determined to build a service that listens and delivers the standard of housing our Armed Forces and their families deserve.

A new Code of Conduct will ensure families receive a more consistent and respectful service from everyone representing Defence housing, including contractors across the supply chain.

A new pilot is also being introduced that will give families a greater role in signing off repairs and maintenance work, helping to ensure issues are fully resolved and work is completed to the expected standard before jobs are closed.

A new Customer Committee will also give families a direct voice in decision-making at a national level, while Regional Experience Committees will bring together residents from across the country to identify local issues and help shape future services. Together, the committees will ensure that family feedback informs decisions across the Defence housing system. This shows the government’s commitment to problem-solving and putting power back into local communities.

Tricia Jakeman, Defence Families Champion, whose role it is to listen to Service families and the challenges they are facing, said:

Behind every military home is a family whose support is essential to operational life. Giving Service families a stronger voice in the decisions that affect them is not only the right thing to do, it is essential if we are to deliver the quality of housing and services they deserve. The changes we’ve seen over the past year show what can be achieved when families are listened to, and this is an important step in ensuring their voices continue to drive positive change.

Behind every military home is a family whose support is essential to operational life. Giving Service families a stronger voice in the decisions that affect them is not only the right thing to do, it is essential if we are to deliver the quality of housing and services they deserve.

The changes we’ve seen over the past year show what can be achieved when families are listened to, and this is an important step in ensuring their voices continue to drive positive change.

The Defence Housing Strategy, launched in November, set out the MOD’s plans to reform military housing over the next decade. Backed by £9.2 billion of investment, it will be delivered through the Defence Housing Service, which will be formally established in April 2027.

Service families can find out more about the Red Tape Challenge and submit their suggestions here: Red Tape Challenge

items.title: French Army wants to keep adversaries guessing on see-through battlefield
items.author: Rudy Ruitenberg
items.summary: The French Future Combat Command is looking at what Baratz called “frugal artificial intelligence,” designed to consume as little energy as possible.
items.body:
Europe

French Army wants to keep adversaries guessing on see-through battlefield

An inflatable decoy of the French Caesar howitzer at the headquarters of France's 7th Armored Brigade in Besançon, France, Sept. 9, 2026. (Rudy Ruitenberg/staff)

BESANÇON, France — The French Army’s Future Combat Command is seeking ways to create “opacity” on an increasingly transparent battlefield in order to restore offensive maneuver , looking at everything from physical decoys to electronic warfare and electromagnetic deception, said Gen. Bruno Baratz , who heads the command.

Battlefield transparency and powerful, precise modern weapons have jointly created a “zone of death” along the frontline where approaching the enemy is “very, very dangerous,” Baratz said at an innovation day held by the French 7th Armored Brigade in eastern France last week. In terms of new technology, what the Army needs most is a way to break the resulting tactical stalemate, he said.

Maneuver along the Ukrainian frontline has largely stalled as near-continuous drone observation means neither Ukraine nor Russia can mass forces without exposing them to destruction. Baratz compared the situation to World War I, when artillery and machine guns meant maneuver and offensive operations could be futile or only possible at the cost of enormous casualties.

“We’re in a system of tactical stalemate, where defensive systems are more powerful than offensive ones,” Baratz said on the sidelines of an innovation day in Besançon on Sept. 9. “We need to be able to break out of this system. So today, we have to be able to recreate what we call a bit of opacity in this world of transparency.”

Baratz said there are “a great number of ways” to think about deception, including physical decoys and electromagnetic deception using simulated command posts. The innovation day featured inflatable copies of equipment used by the 7th Armored Brigade, including a Caesar howitzer and the VBL light armored vehicle.

The commander also noted the importance of electromagnetic jamming, and of electronic warfare and cyber warfare as forces become increasingly connected.

“How can we blind the adversary? How do we mislead him about our intentions? How can we create a temporary vulnerability with the adversary to restore momentum and offensive action,” Baratz said.

“Above all, how do we deceive his sensors or ensure that his sensors don’t see the right things, allowing the concentration of force? Because today, we can’t concentrate if we’re destroyed, and so there isn’t the mass necessary to be able to throw the adversary off balance.”

Other technologies that could reshape the battlefield include quantum technology, both for secure communications as well as for sensing, according to Baratz.

“There’s also multi-spectral image analysis that is starting to allow us to see what’s under trees, what’s under cover,” the general said. “There are new technologies, often driven by artificial intelligence, that provide capabilities we couldn’t have imagined until now.”

With the pace of technological change in some areas now measured in weeks rather than years or months, that creates difficulties for the military, according to Baratz. He cited telecommunications, where the military is “lagging far behind” the civilian sector in terms of bandwidth and data transmission capacity, even as the modern battlefield is organized around data.

The general said the military may be on the brink of a revolution in warfare similar to that of 1920, when mechanization and radio communications accelerated the pace of maneuver. The growing use of data on the battlefield may ultimately speed up both decision-making and destruction of the adversary, Baratz said.

Baratz said the modern battlefield has “radically changed” from the past, when military tactics were ultimately organized around geography, “that is to say the ridge line that defined the field of fire or field of view.”

“So how do we reinvent ourselves tactically?” Baratz said. “At the time, we French didn’t really reinvent ourselves, and we paid the price in 1940.”

Baratz said innovation has become an element of operational superiority for armies, and the ability to continuously adapt systems and incorporate new technology is fundamental.

The Future Combat Command has therefore adopted “a logic that is entirely different” from the Army’s traditional top-down approach, and is encouraging “testing, tinkering, experimenting” at the regimental level, Baratz said, with the aim of making the force more efficient, more flexible, more adaptable and more creative.

While large-scale programs will remain necessary, the Army also needs to be able to repurpose civilian technologies for military purposes and increasingly move toward open-architecture systems, Baratz said.

The Army currently provides each regiment with €150,000 ($172,000) a year to spend on their own projects or to buy off-the-shelf kit in a bid to stimulate grassroots innovation. The Army’s €20 million account for these “subsidiarity credits” is being increased with an additional €35 million in the 2027 defense budget, according to Baratz.

The commander said the Army has “real needs” in areas including robotics, autonomous vehicles, discreet mobility and battlefield-energy generation. New companies are entering the market in those areas and reaching out to the French forces, including increasingly European firms, which is helping stimulate thinking and the wider ecosystem, Baratz said.

He said all French brigades have initiatives around light mobility, working with companies on electric scooters, motorcycles and quads to be “faster and stealthier on this changing battlefield.”

Electric power allows forces to be more discreet but is also an area of vulnerability, due to the need for intelligence-gathering systems and frontline data hubs that are all power hungry, the general said. The Future Combat Command is therefore also looking at what Baratz called “frugal artificial intelligence,” designed to consume as little energy as possible.

“All of this is the combat of the future,” Baratz said. “It’s the future combat that remains hard to imagine, because technology is moving so quickly that I’m incapable of telling you what things will look like in one or two years.”

Rudy Ruitenberg is a Europe correspondent for Defense News. He started his career at Bloomberg News and has experience reporting on technology, commodity markets and politics.

items.title: A Design Lab Pilot to Inform Strategies for Expanding Access to Medications for Opioid Use Disorder in Community Mental Health Centers
items.author: Bradley D. Stein
items.summary: A pilot Design Lab identified barriers and strategies to improving access to medications for opioid use disorder in community mental health settings. Expanding insurer reimbursement via a learning exchange was seen as most impactful and feasible.
items.body:
Allison J. Ober , Sarah B. Hunter , Alex R. Dopp , Bradley D. Stein

Research Published Sep 18, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

This pilot Design Lab engaged clients, clinic leaders, and policy experts to identify barriers and strategies for expanding access to medications for opioid use disorder. Stigma, workforce shortages, regulatory complexity, and payment limitations emerged as key challenges. Expanding insurer reimbursement through a structured learning exchange was rated highest in impact and feasibility, suggesting cross-sector collaboration may advance access.

Opportunities outside the technology and innovation space can be found at Procurement at MOD .

Guidance for new suppliers

These are usually set up to help government buy a specific type of product or service, and have standard terms and processes which make it easier to contract with us. Once you are on a framework you can apply for any advertised opportunities until the framework ends.

Some frameworks are ‘open’, which means they can be joined at any time, while others are only open during certain periods. There are also Dynamic markets which are continuously open for new suppliers to join, making it simpler and faster to access contract opportunities.

items.title: US Air Force to extend service of B-1, B-2 bombers, official says
items.author: Cristina Stassis
items.summary: The service lives of the B-1 Lancer and B-2 Spirit will be extended, with their pilots to be some of the first to fly the B-21 Raider.
items.body:
MilTech

US Air Force to extend service of B-1, B-2 bombers, official says

People photograph a U.S. Air Force B-1 as it approaches to land at RAF Fairford, Gloucestershire, Britain, March 17, 2026. (Toby Melville/Reuters)

Two of the U.S. Air Force’s bomber aircraft will be extended in an effort to better maintain the fleet’s readiness, a service official said Wednesday.

The decision to extend the B-1 Lancer and B-2 Spirit comes amid moves by the force to further develop the B-21 Raider, the service’s next-generation stealth bomber with accelerated production.

Both the bombers will be extended, Gen. Stephen L. Davis, commander of the Air Force Global Strike Command, said during a panel titled “Flying and Fixing to Fight and Win” at the Air & Space Forces Association’s 2026 Air, Space & Cyber Conference .

The commander said that the experienced pilots from the bombers will be some of the first B-21 pilots.

The Raiders are on track for a 2027 delivery to Ellsworth Air Force Base, South Dakota. The service aims to replace the aging B-1 and B-2 fleets in the coming decades with at least 100 B-21s.

Davis highlighted the Air Force’s Bomber Supplemental Trainer for Aircrew Readiness, or BSTAR , program, which is meant to address gaps and flight-hour readiness for B-1 pilots. In the program, XSTAR Aviation provides the force with HondaJet Elite light business jets.

“We’re bringing in a HondaJet to actually help experience some pilots, and also as some of these airframes have issues with readiness, it gives those pilots a chance to fly and get them time in the seat, which we know is very important,” Davis said during the panel.

The commander didn’t say how long the bombers’ service lives would be extended for, but the service intends to modernize and invest in the B-1 and B-2s in the coming years despite both aircraft being slated for retirement in the next decade.

Recently, the service launched an operation readiness campaign, dubbed the North Star Readiness Campaign , to increase the number of mission-capable B-52 Stratofortress and B-1s by accelerating the delivery of parts, engineering support and depot maintenance.

During the campaign’s announcement, the force said that while the B-52 and B-1 are being upgraded to continue service, the B-2 will be maintained for combat effectiveness until the B-21 is fully operational.

Cristina Stassis is a reporter covering stories surrounding the defense industry, national security, military/veteran affairs and more. She previously worked as an editorial fellow for Defense News in 2024 where she assisted the newsroom in breaking news across Sightline Media Group.

items.title: The US Army is looking for new drones to ferry blood supplies
items.author: Michael Peck
items.summary: As part of the U.S. Army Blood Link project, the service is seeking new drones that can transport blood supplies in the field.
items.body:
MilTech

The US Army is looking for new drones to ferry blood supplies

Soldiers change the batteries of a drone during a drone-based blood resupply as part of the multinational Hospital Exercise. (Sgt. Jose Lora/Army)

The U.S. Army is looking for drones that can transport blood supplies in the field, according to a new sources sought notice from the service.

The Army aims to select a contractor that can deliver two prototype UAVs for what it is calling the Army Blood Link project, the notice states. Each drone must be capable of transporting 20 units of blood products.

The deadline to respond to the notice is Sept. 21, and the drones will need to be delivered within three months of the contract award.

“Due to the compressed timeline, we recommend focusing on further development and adaptation of existing commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) UAS solutions,” the notice emphasized.

The request for proposals, issued on behalf of the XVIII Airborne Corps Joint Operations Innovation Outpost, calls for a UAV that can haul a minimum of 35 pounds and up to 50 pounds. The drone should have a one-way transport radius of 30 kilometers and a maximum range of 100 kilometers, the notice states.

Maximum speed was not specified in the request, but the Army wants a UAV capable of flying at an altitude of up to 18,000 feet. The request notes that the UAV should also be capable of a “maximum 30-minute response time from mission request to launch under standard operating conditions.”

Given the perishability of blood supplies, the drone must carefully regulate its operating temperature, the Army requested. The cargo container should “maintain required temperature for up to [three] hours of transport time, within an ambient environment of 15°F to 120°F with high humidity,” the notice states.

The Army estimates a total mission duration of three to six hours, with blood carried within temperature limits for no more than three hours.

The request also details that the container must accommodate blood bags roughly 8 inches long and 5 inches wide. The cargo bay should also be resistant to vibration, rain, sand, chemical contamination and other environmental hazards.

Upon delivery, the drone will need to precisely land a cargo within 10 meters of the desired location, according to the request.

Potentially dropping of the blood supplies from the air is also possible, the notice states. This would mean a “drop capability from 10 to 15 meters above ground level with landing accuracy sufficient to remain within the 10-meter delivery-location requirement and not damage the blood products or compromise container integrity,” the request notes.

The Army envisions a semi-autonomous drone with “autonomous waypoint navigation and return-to-base functions, under operator supervision.” The service wants the UAV and its ground equipment to also have an operational lifespan of 500 to 1,500 flight hours.

The Army has been devoting more attention to the challenge of delivering blood supplies to the front lines. In May 2025, the 173rd Airborne Brigade used drones to transport blood during the Swift Response exercise in Lithuania.

Michael Peck is a correspondent for Defense News and a columnist for the Center for European Policy Analysis. He holds an M.A. in political science from Rutgers University. Find him at theuncommondefense.com. His email is mikedefense1@gmail.com.

items.title: Preserving Jobs and Tax Revenue in the Age of AI: Q&A with Carter Price
items.summary: Carter Price, a mathematician at RAND and co-director of the RAND Von Furstenberg Family Budget Model Initiative, discusses ways to rebalance the tax code so that it doesn't incentivize employers to replace humans with AI.
items.body:
Preserving Jobs and Tax Revenue in the Age of AI: Q&A with Carter Price

Commentary

Sep 17, 2026

If AI starts to replace jobs, it isn't just American workers who will feel the loss of income. So will the U.S. Treasury.

Nearly two-thirds of all federal revenue comes from taxes levied on human labor, a recent RAND study noted. That revenue will not be easy to make up if AI starts to put large numbers of people out of work.

Carter Price has been looking for ways to rebalance the tax code so that it doesn't incentivize employers to replace humans with AI. He's a mathematician at RAND and co-director of the RAND Von Furstenberg Family Budget Model Initiative . And he has an idea for how to give workers an edge in the age of AI.

How does the existing tax code disincentivize keeping human workers on the job?

We went through all 7,000 pages of the tax code with a tool we built as part of the RAND Budget Model Initiative. It allows us to identify every provision, every line item, and its implications. There's a lot in there. But we identified several places where the existing U.S tax code works against companies hiring or keeping workers.

The employer payroll tax is one obvious example. Companies have to pay that tax for every worker they hire, so more workers means more expense. Meanwhile, the tax code allows companies to write off the depreciation of big, expensive assets early, before those assets actually wear out. That can make buying something like a robotic system much more cost-effective—which makes that tax write-off a direct subsidy for displacing human workers.

What's your idea to change the incentives here?

You and I pay progressive taxes on our income. That means if we make more money, we move into a higher tax bracket.

Our idea is somewhat similar, but for companies. The government would tax high corporate profits per worker in addition to taxing their income overall.

Imagine a company makes $1 million in profit and has 100 employees. Its profit per worker is $10,000. Now let's say that company brings in a lot of AI and lays off all but ten of its workers. Now its profit per worker is $100,000, and it just moved into a higher tax bracket. It's going to pay more in taxes for that same $1 million in profit.

AI might still be so much more efficient that it still makes sense for some companies to replace those workers. This tax structure wouldn't stand in the way of that.

But where the current tax code sometimes disincentivizes keeping human workers, our proposed change would flip the script. It would put the tax code more on the side of workers instead of on the side of AI and automation.

What else did your tax code analysis find that could help promote employment?

We found a lot of special, niche provisions that are just scattered throughout the tax code. You could eliminate those and really clean everything up. There are three different clean-energy vehicle tax provisions, for example, and they all do pretty much the same thing.

These niche provisions pointed us to a suite of changes that could really make a difference. The government could eliminate those special tax breaks. That would bring in additional revenue.

The federal government could then eliminate the employer payroll tax and replace it with two business taxes: one a flat tax on business revenue, and the other the per-worker tax on high profits.

Companies would be no worse off. The government would balance the loss of revenue from eliminating the payroll tax with an increase from eliminating special tax carve-outs. And we'd be incentivizing human employment instead of using tax breaks to incentivize things like investments in distilled spirits.

Our proposed change would put the tax code more on the side of workers instead of on the side of AI and automation.

What would it take to implement those changes?

It takes an act of Congress to change the Internal Revenue Code. But that's a low barrier compared to what some other popular policy ideas that are floating around would face. For example, a value-added tax, which would be like a nationwide sales tax, would require an entirely new tax-collection infrastructure. And a federal wealth tax, which could generate revenue from huge concentrations of wealth, would require a constitutional amendment in addition to new tax-collection infrastructure.

By contrast, policymakers could at least theoretically wake up tomorrow and pass a law that would make the tax code more robust by reducing its dependence on income from labor.

Furthermore, simplifying the tax code would give people back millions of hours that they currently spend filling out forms. It would improve the efficiency of the economy, and that's something everyone can like.

What motivates you to do this work?

I'm a mathematician. And there have been a lot of headlines about the advances that AI models have made in mathematics in particular. AI can generate code that would take a human hours, or even days, to write. I'm biased, but I think human mathematicians still provide a lot of value that AI can't fully replace. I'm not sure that will be true forever. But until that changes, we shouldn't rush into replacing workers with AI, and our tax code certainly shouldn't incentivize employers to do so.

items.title: Legal and Clinical Liability of Comanaging Pediatric Mental Health With Unregulated AI Chatbots
items.author: Hao Yu
items.summary: We conclude that parents and clinicians should proactively discuss chatbot use to promote safety, appropriate expectations, and linkages to evidence-based care.
items.body:
Reply

Ryan K. McBain , Jonathan H. Cantor , Hao Yu

Research Posted on rand.org Sep 16, 2026 Published in: JAMA Pediatrics (2026). DOI: 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2026.3929

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

In Reply: We thank Lennon for highlighting an issue that requires serious legal and policy attention as adolescents increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots for mental health advice. However, we believe the letter rests on a premise that mischaracterizes the conclusions of our article.1 We did not recommend clinicians comanage, police, or actively integrate unregulated chatbots into pediatric mental health care. Rather, we reported that nearly 1 in 5 US adolescents and young adults had used AI chatbots for mental health advice, that most users found them helpful, and that 63.3% disclosed this use to no one. On that basis, we concluded that parents and clinicians should proactively discuss chatbot use to promote safety, appropriate expectations, and linkages to evidence-based care.

items.title: Describing Neighborhood-Level Disparities in Pediatric Firearm Injuries
items.author: Terry L. Schell
items.summary: The authors conduct a ZIP code level analysis of pediatric firearm injuries and deaths across the United States and their correlation with a range of neighborhood and state-level factors.
items.body:
Andrew R. Morral , Terry L. Schell

Research Posted on rand.org Sep 16, 2026 Published in: Pediatrics, e2026076245 (2026). DOI: 10.1542/peds.2026-076245

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Pediatric firearm injuries and mortality concentrate in states or urban neighborhoods with high rates of poverty, unemployment, racial segregation, family instability, and other measures of social vulnerability; permissive gun laws; and reduced access to quality health care, education, and recreational opportunities. In this issue of Pediatrics, Diaz and colleagues reaffirm these findings with a ZIP code level analysis of pediatric firearm injuries and deaths across the United States and their correlation with a range of neighborhood and state-level factors.

items.title: Army Chaplains’ Perceptions About Identifying, Intervening, and Referring Soldiers at Risk of Suicide
items.author: Aaron Kofner
items.summary: In this study, we estimate perceptions of Army chaplains and CAs in domains relevant to gatekeeping, including intervention efficacy, reluctance to intervene, stigma, and past intervention behavior.
items.body:
Rajeev Ramchand , Lynsay Ayer , Lily Geyer , Aaron Kofner

Research Posted on rand.org Sep 16, 2026 Published in: Spirituality in Clinical Practice, Volume 2, No. 1, pages 36-47 (March 2015). DOI: 10.1037/scp0000053

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

In U.S. Army policy, chaplains and chaplain assistants (CAs) are explicitly identified as primary gatekeepers; however, research on their perceptions about their roles identifying, caring for, and referring soldiers in suicidal distress is scant. In this study, we estimate perceptions of Army chaplains and CAs in domains relevant to gatekeeping, including intervention efficacy, reluctance to intervene, stigma, and past intervention behavior. We do so using an online survey that was administered to all chaplains and CAs in the Army’s Active Component and Reserves in 2012. Response rates ranged from 41% of all chaplains in the Active Component to 19% of chaplains and CAs in the Reserves. Almost half of all chaplains and CAs thought they could use more suicide prevention training. Although chaplains reported greater perceived ability to intervene with individuals at risk for suicide relative to civilian samples, they also reported more reluctance to intervene. This reluctance may be explained in part by high reports of stigma regarding mental health treatment. These findings suggest that the Army should implement specific suicide prevention training for chaplains and CAs that focuses on providing acute behavioral health treatment, reducing mental health stigma, and encouraging chaplains to collaborate with other behavioral health resources.

items.title: Evolving Health and Wellbeing of Thalidomide Survivors as They Age
items.author: Agne Ulyte
items.summary: This scoping review updates the 2017 review by exploring evidence published 2017-2025 on the physical, mental, and social wellbeing of ageing thalidomide survivors, identifying emerging health issues, care needs, and evidence gaps.
items.body:
A Scoping Review Update (2017-2025)

Sorana Bucseneanu , Elizabeth Newbronner , Sarah Nettleton , Jennifer Bousfield , Agne Ulyte

Research Posted on rand.org Sep 16, 2026 Published in: Disabilities, Volume 6, Issue 4 (August 2026). DOI: 10.3390/disabilities6040067

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Background

Thalidomide, prescribed to pregnant women in the late 1950s and early 1960s, caused severe congenital impairments known as thalidomide embryopathy, yet the long-term health and wellbeing of survivors as they reach older adulthood remains underexplored.

Objectives

This scoping review updates the 2017 Newbronner and Atkin review by exploring evidence published between 2017 and 2025 on the physical, mental, and social wellbeing of ageing thalidomide survivors, identifying emerging health issues, care needs, and evidence gaps.

Methods

Searches across nine academic databases and grey literature sources identified studies reporting health, wellbeing, or quality of life among middle-aged and older adults with documented prenatal thalidomide exposure.

Results

Thirty papers from the UK, Germany, Japan, Italy, Sweden, Canada, and Australia were included, showing pervasive musculoskeletal deterioration, chronic pain, and increased metabolic disorders. Mental health conditions, including depression, anxiety, and stress, were common and often linked to pain severity and functional limitations, alongside sensory impairments, dental issues, and functional decline, though many survivors demonstrated resilience.

Conclusions

Ageing thalidomide survivors face complex, progressive health challenges that extend beyond congenital impairments, highlighting a need for coordinated, specialist care to support wellbeing in later life.

items.title: Do Stigma and Efficacy Mediate the Association Between Training and Suicide Prevention Behavior Among Army Noncommissioned Officers?
items.author: Lisa Wagner
items.summary: We surveyed Army NCOs to determine if training on suicide prevention and soft skills was associated with gatekeeper behavior and use of soft skills, and whether that association was explained by stigma and perceptions of efficacy.
items.body:
Stephanie Brooks Holliday , Lynsay Ayer , Robin L. Beckman , Lisa H. Jaycox , Denis Agniel , Daniel Elinoff , Rajeev Ramchand , Lisa Wagner

Research Posted on rand.org Sep 16, 2026 Published in: Suicide and Life-Threatening Behavior, Volume 54, Issue 2, pages 195-206 (April 2024). DOI: 10.1111/sltb.13033

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Introduction

Rates of suicide in the Active Component of the military have significantly increased since 2010, with particularly high rates among Army service members. One element of the Army's approach to suicide prevention relies on noncommissioned officers (NCOs) as gatekeepers who have regular contact with soldiers. NCOs receive suicide prevention training, but there is limited evidence that such training leads to behavior change.

Methods

We surveyed 2468 Army NCOs participating in leadership development courses to determine (a) if training on suicide prevention and soft skills (e.g., active listening) was associated with gatekeeper behavior and use of soft skills; and (b) whether that association was explained by two potential barriers, stigma and perceptions of efficacy.

Results

Both the number of suicide prevention training topics and soft skills trained were associated with increased gatekeeper behavior; these relationships were explained in part by lower stigma and higher efficacy for use of soft skills. The use of interactive training methods and receiving coaching after training were not associated with stigma or efficacy, though both methods were associated with more frequent use of soft skills.

Conclusion

Results suggest that the content and format of training is important to preparing NCOs to fulfill a gatekeeper role.

items.title: Preventing the Creation of Mirror Life
items.author: Krista Langeland
items.summary: This brief summarizes RAND research on steps the United States could take to prevent the creation of mirror life—a synthetic life form that could pose irreversible risks—before the window for meaningful action closes.
items.body:
A Strategy for the United States

Nidhi Kalra , Forrest W. Crawford , Matthew L. Nicotra , Scott Behmer , Josh Dettman , Gerald L. Epstein , Edward Geist , David Glickstein , Graham Griffin , Krista Langeland

Research Summary Published Sep 16, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

The creation of mirror life—a hypothetical life form, such as a bacterium, built from biomolecules with the opposite molecular structure of all known life on earth—could cause fatal infections in multicellular life, including humans, animals, and plants, and upend entire ecosystems. In July 2026, RAND published A U.S. Strategy to Prevent the Creation of Mirror Life , which overviews two lines of effort (LOEs) that U.S. policymakers could pursue to prevent mirror life from becoming reality. This brief summarizes these LOEs, the policy levers called for by each LOE, and the principles and analysis on which they are built.

Mirror Life: What It Is and How It Could Pose Catastrophic Risk

Mirror life is a hypothetical form of life built from biomolecules with the opposite molecular structure of all known life on earth. Although mirror life does not yet exist, experts estimate that creation of the first mirror bacterium—a likely first instantiation of mirror life—could be technically feasible within the next few decades and could potentially cost as little as several hundred million dollars.

Mirror life’s reverse molecular structure could enable mirror bacteria to (1) escape immune detection and cause fatal infections, (2) avoid natural predators, and (3) proliferate throughout natural ecosystems. If created and released, whether accidentally or intentionally, mirror bacteria could potentially spread widely, causing irreversible harm.

The Policy Challenge: Preventing an Irreversible Threshold

The policy challenge that mirror life presents is both urgent and unusual. Scientists have produced mirror-image biomolecules that could serve as the building blocks of mirror life. Much of the research that moves science closer to realizing mirror bacteria is not inherently dangerous, has demonstrated benefits or promises benefits, and is likely to continue for reasons unrelated to the creation of mirror life. However, mirror life itself is expected to have few plausible benefits. Despite this, some actors might still wish to pursue mirror life, such as well-intentioned researchers who overlook the risks associated with mirror life or malicious actors who seek to acquire or use mirror life as a doomsday capability.

Traditional governance approaches for emerging technologies—such as post-hoc regulation or adaptive oversight—rely on the opportunity to mitigate risks as they emerge and before they become crises. These approaches might be ill-suited to govern mirror life. This is because once a single viable mirror bacterium exists, the knowledge and methods for making riskier variants could proliferate rapidly, and even seemingly benign strains of such bacteria could be modified to be more dangerous. The first successful creation of mirror life could therefore represent an irreversible threshold: a point after which containment and control become far more difficult and perhaps even impossible.

A Global Challenge Requiring U.S. Leadership

Only a small number of scientifically advanced actors possess the capacity to pursue mirror life. For the foreseeable future, less advanced actors—including isolated or sanctioned regimes, nonstate groups, and individuals—lack the infrastructure, expertise, and access to materials that are required to create mirror life without assistance from the global scientific community. This asymmetry has an important strategic implication: Should the few scientific powers capable of creating mirror life agree on the need to prevent it, their restraint effectively denies the means of creating it to all others.

The United States, as one of the world’s leading scientific powers and a global hub for bioscience and biotechnology, is uniquely positioned to influence the global trajectory of mirror life development and therefore should lead international efforts to prevent its creation. U.S. actions can help establish international restraint, although preventing mirror life ultimately depends on sustained cooperation among the major scientific powers—particularly China—because no country can manage the risk alone.

Four Principles for a U.S. Strategy

RAND researchers guided U.S. policymakers in developing a strategy to address the risks posed by mirror life before scientific progress or geopolitical incentives close the window for meaningful action. Rather than predicting whether mirror life will pose catastrophic risk with certainty, the authors treat the expert assessment that mirror life could pose unacceptable risks as sufficient motivation for strategic planning now.

RAND researchers identified the following four principles, which guide the development of a strategy:

Prevention over mitigation: Because the first mirror bacterium could trigger irreversible consequences and enable the rapid proliferation of mirror life capabilities, governance, norms, and constraints must be established before mirror life exists—rather than governments and other actors relying on mitigation after the fact.

Universal restraint over partial restraint: Even a single actor creating mirror life could pose a global risk. Prevention depends on broadly shared restraint supported by coordinated governance, transparency, and scientific norms.

Transparency over secrecy: A shared understanding of mirror life’s risks and confidence that others are exercising restraint are essential for preventing competitive dynamics and sustaining collective prevention efforts.

Cooperation over coercion: Because no country can eliminate the risk alone, prevention requires trusted international cooperation that preserves legitimacy and encourages broad participation rather than coercive measures.

Two Lines of Effort: Reducing Incentives and Advancing Detection and Deterrence

RAND researchers identified policy levers that policymakers could consider, specifically those that (1) reduce incentives to develop mirror life and (2) detect and deter early-stage development of mirror life. Other levers—such as those that disrupt or punish advanced development or build countermeasures and resilience—are inconsistent with the four strategic principles and therefore do not factor into a U.S. preventive strategy.

The U.S. strategy organizes levers into the following LOEs (Figure 1):

LOE 1—Engage scientific superpowers, especially China, to build the foundation for collective restraint. This LOE prioritizes transparent scientific collaboration, shared risk assessments, and early norm-setting to discourage major powers from viewing mirror life as a strategic advantage and to prevent mirror life research from becoming an arena for geopolitical competition. LOE 1 shapes the incentives for major scientific powers and academic institutions and has a cascading impact on other nation-states and commercial firms. Although LOE 1’s direct influence on other actors is more limited, broadly stigmatizing mirror life could still create reputational and operational barriers for malign actors.

LOE 2—Establish collective restraint across domestic, allied, and competing scientific communities. This LOE combines measures that reduce the incentives and increase the costs of creating mirror life. Together, these actions shift motivations and capabilities away from mirror life development for states, commercial firms, research institutions, and multilateral bodies.

In pursuing these LOEs, the United States should:

Commit clearly to not developing mirror life, even if other actors are suspected of pursuing it. This commitment reflects the fact that the possession of mirror life would not provide protection, deterrence, or resilience against mirror life developed by others and would instead exacerbate global risk.

Take great caution with actions or statements that could foster mistrust or spur strategic competition in the field of mirror life or its enabling technologies, particularly actions or statements that are related to disrupting mirror life development or investing in countermeasures and resilience.

Advance actions with longer lead times as soon as possible. Legislation, international engagement, technology development for detection and verification, and treaty-creation groundwork require years to mature. These efforts should begin now and evolve as new information emerges.

Exclude coercive measures from the strategy at this time. Actions that rely on pressure, disruption, or punishment would erode trust and cooperation among major scientific powers on which prevention depends. Such measures should be out of scope at this time. If such measures ever become appropriate, they should be pursued cooperatively and transparently, not unilaterally.

Treat countermeasures and resilience as later-resort measures. These measures are unlikely to be effective against the proliferation of mirror life and the ensuing risks. Premature or unilateral investment in defensive preparations could inadvertently weaken deterrence, advance the science of mirror life, and trigger counterproductive dynamics.

By strengthening trust, transparency, and cooperative incentives, the United States can help ensure that those with the means to develop mirror life choose not to—and, in doing so, make mirror life’s pursuit infeasible for everyone else.

items.title: The Insurability of Artificial Intelligence
items.author: Celine Robinson
items.summary: A mismatch exists between rapid enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) and the market for insuring it. This report examines AI incidents, lawsuits, laws, and insurance filings to assess coverage responses and accumulation risks.
items.body:
A mismatch exists between rapid enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) and the fragmented market for insuring AI-related losses. This report examines AI incidents, U.S. lawsuits, enacted state laws, and insurance filings to assess how insurers are responding through exclusions, endorsements, affirmative coverage, or silence.

The Insurability of Artificial Intelligence

Sasha Romanosky , Celine Robinson

Research Published Sep 16, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Businesses increasingly embed artificial intelligence (AI) in operations, products, and services, creating both new opportunities and new forms of risk. Firms are deploying AI in customer service, employment screening, coding, fraud detection, and autonomous systems. At the same time, AI-related harms are already emerging, including incorrect or misleading outputs, deepfakes, privacy violations, intellectual property disputes, fraud, product defects, and discriminatory decisions. These harms create demand for insurance but do not fit neatly within existing insurance lines.

In this report, the authors examine AI incidents, U.S. lawsuits, enacted state laws, and admitted-market insurance filings to assess how insurers are responding through exclusions, endorsements, affirmative coverage, or silence. Key findings include the dominance of misinformation incidents, concentration of litigation around intellectual property, and five mechanisms through which AI could generate accumulation losses across insurance lines.

Key Takeaways

Of public generative AI incidents, 84 percent relate to misinformation (false, deceptive, or manipulative content) and deepfakes (AI-generated or altered media impersonating a real person or event).

Of U.S. litigation for generative AI harms, 60 percent relate to the alleged violations of intellectual property or improper training by AI developers rather than to the use, misuse, or outputs of these models.

Most U.S. states have adopted laws focusing on restricting harmful synthetic content, such as nonconsensual intimate images and child sexual abuse material.

Unlike cyber, AI risks are not contained to a single insurance line but span many lines: technology errors and omissions and professional liability, cyber, directors and officers, commercial property, and more.

Insurance carriers are responding to AI risks unevenly, with some offering affirmative coverage for certain risks (e.g., model errors), and others filing broad exclusions for any AI-related loss.

Most carriers are remaining silent, neither affirming nor excluding AI-related risks in their policies, leaving coverage for such losses untested and open to dispute.

Recommendations

State insurance regulators and the National Association of Insurance Commissioners, supported by carriers and brokers, should develop an AI Coverage Notice enabling carriers to clarify how, and under which lines, AI-related losses are affirmatively covered, excluded, or left silent.

Incident reporting for attritional and accumulation loss should be standardized. Policy researchers and brokers, together with carriers and reinsurers, should develop a common, adaptable taxonomy for AI incidents, claims, and controls to properly track and report on AI risks. Actual incident data should remain private, however.

Insurers and reinsurers should analyze AI aggregation scenarios, focusing on shared model dependency, common infrastructure failure, and regulatory shock to manage correlated AI risk.

The Mid-Atlantic Regional Climate Impacts Summary and Outlook is a quarterly series produced by the Mid-Atlantic Regional Integrated Science and Assessments (MARISA) program, a collaboration funded by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration through the RAND Corporation and researchers at Pennsylvania State University, Carnegie Mellon University, Johns Hopkins University, Morgan State University, Cornell University, and the Virginia Institute of Marine Science. This series draws information from regional climate centers, news and weather information, and high-resolution climate data sets for the benefit of policymakers, practitioners, residents, and community leaders in the Mid-Atlantic region, with a focus on the Chesapeake Bay watershed. Projections of future climate in the Mid-Atlantic region come from the best available scientific information. For this summer 2026 version of the series, Part 1 details significant weather events that occurred from June through August 2026; Part 2 characterizes seasonal temperature and precipitation compared to historical averages; Part 3 describes seasonal weather forecasts and pertinent information for the upcoming fall season; and Part four provides a primer on the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO), how it will impact weather in the Mid-Atlantic and how it is projected to change in the future.

items.title: Positioning Qatar in the Global Research, Development, and Innovation Landscape
items.author: Sara Zikri
items.summary: Qatar aims to strengthen its research, development, and innovation (RDI) ecosystem. This report benchmarks Qatar against other small advanced economies and identifies policy options to close gaps in STEM talent, research, and innovation capacity.
items.body:
Qatar aims to strengthen its research, development, and innovation (RDI) ecosystem. This report benchmarks Qatar against other small advanced economies, examines international policy practices, and evaluates its national strategies. It identifies weak STEM interest, fragmented researcher support, retention challenges linked to short visas, and limited industry–academia collaboration, and sets out policy options to address these gaps.

Positioning Qatar in the Global Research, Development, and Innovation Landscape

Comparative Insights from Small Advanced Economies

Mehdi Shiva , James Besse , Stella Harrison , Miguel Subosa , Ishita Puri , Paul Khullar , Abdellahi Hussein , Sara Zikri

Research Published Sep 16, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Qatar has articulated a bold vision to strengthen its research, development, and innovation (RDI) ecosystem, as set out in the Third National Development Strategy and the Qatar Research Development and Innovation Council's 2030 Strategy. These strategies set ambitious targets for expanding the RDI talent pool, raising government investment in research and innovation, and improving outputs such as high-impact publications, patents and start-ups.

This report assesses the current state of Qatar's RDI ecosystem by benchmarking performance indicators against other small, advanced economies, examining international policy practices, and evaluating the effects of Qatar's national strategies on research and innovation outcomes. It highlights areas of relative strength and identifies policy options to address persistent gaps.

The most significant challenge identified is the relatively low level of interest and attainment in STEM disciplines among Qatari students, which weakens the domestic talent pipeline. Although national strategies recognise the importance of STEM education, a comprehensive and coordinated action plan is lacking. Support for early-career researchers is also fragmented, and retention of skilled international talent is constrained by short visa durations and limited employment flexibility. Collaboration between research institutions and the private sector remains limited, restricting the translation of knowledge into innovation.

The study finds that the Qatar National Vision 2030 has positively influenced research and innovation outputs, even amid regional and global disruptions, and the more recent QRDI 2030 Strategy shows early signs of effectiveness, though it is too soon to assess its full impact. Future evaluations should incorporate broader indicators and longitudinal data.

Key Takeaways

Industry–academia collaboration is limited

Linkages between research institutions and the private sector remain weak, constraining the translation of knowledge into innovation. While the business set-up process is relatively streamlined, set-up costs have been high relative to comparator economies, standing at 6.3% of GNI per capita in 2019, though recent developments suggest significant reductions. Against a backdrop of declining total factor productivity, revitalising the private sector through entrepreneurship and innovation is increasingly important. Existing infrastructure such as QSTP and Education City offers a foundation on which closer co-location and coordination between academia and industry can be built.

Researcher development and retention need targeted attention

Support for early-career researchers is fragmented and administered largely by individual universities, producing variable training quality. Recent visa reforms, including the Mustaqel visa and the abandonment of the Kafala system, have improved conditions for migrant researchers, but short visa durations and limited employment flexibility continue to push international talent away, often before researchers can secure subsequent employment.

STEM interest and attainment remain weak

The relatively low level of interest and attainment in STEM disciplines among Qatari students weakens the domestic talent pipeline and limits capacity to meet future workforce demands. Despite improvements in attainment over the past decade, Qatar continues to underperform in science and mathematics relative to other small, advanced economies. National strategies acknowledge STEM's importance, but no concrete, coordinated action plan is in place.

Recommendations

A more coordinated approach to STEM education

Qatar may wish to consider a coordinated STEM action plan spanning early to adult education, with clearer roles and stronger teacher development. Finland and New Zealand's teacher-led communities of practice offer useful reference points.

Supporting researcher development and retention

There may be value in exploring a nationally administered fellowship scheme for early-career researchers, drawing on Singapore's approach, alongside greater visa flexibility informed by models such as Ireland's.

Deepening industry–academia collaboration

Building on QSTP and Education City, Qatar could consider cluster-based approaches, with QRDI well placed to help coordinate and evaluate support.

items.title: Research, development, and innovation talent in Qatar
items.author: Sara Zikri
items.summary: Qatar aims to become a global hub for research, development, and innovation (RDI). This report reviews international approaches to developing, attracting, and retaining RDI talent, examining Qatar's landscape and identifying gaps and opportunities.
items.body:
Qatar aims to become a global hub for research, development, and innovation (RDI). This report examines its RDI talent landscape and reviews international approaches to developing, attracting, and retaining skilled professionals. It finds strong investment in talent development, but persistent retention challenges linked to short visa durations and precarious employment, and identifies opportunities to deepen academia–industry collaboration.

Research, development, and innovation talent in Qatar

The policy and program Landscape

Mehdi Shiva , James Besse , Stella Harrison , Miguel Subosa , Ishita Puri , Abdellahi Hussein , Sara Zikri

Research Published Sep 16, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Qatar has set out an ambitious vision to become a global hub for research, development, and innovation (RDI), underpinned by the recognition that human capital is the foundation of a knowledge-based economy. This report examines Qatar's RDI talent landscape, reviews international approaches to developing, attracting, and retaining skilled professionals, and identifies key gaps and opportunities.

As countries compete intensely for high-skilled labour amid accelerating technological change and ageing populations, RDI talent has become a vital strategic asset underpinning productivity and competitiveness. Qatar's ecosystem has evolved rapidly: gross expenditure on research and development rose from 0.48% to 0.68% of GDP between 2012 and 2021, though it remains well below the OECD average of 2.7%. The workforce is predominantly expatriate, with around 80% of RDI personnel being non-nationals, and only about 7% of Qataris hold STEM qualifications.

To address these challenges, Qatar has introduced initiatives that broadly mirror international good practice, spanning scholarships and mentorship, research placements, incubation and venture funding, and policy reforms aligning education with labour-market priorities. Measures to attract global talent include a forthcoming long-term residency visa offering renewable residence to highly skilled individuals without pre-arranged sponsorship. Persistent challenges remain, however, including limited post-fellowship employment continuity, short visa durations, and constrained academic career pathways.

Achieving Qatar's 2030 workforce targets, including 46% of employment in skilled occupations and at least 18% of graduates in STEM disciplines, will require deeper academia–industry collaboration, diversified RDI funding, and strengthened career and residency frameworks.

Key Takeaways

RDI talent strategies cluster around three objectives

International policies and programmes pursue three broad aims: developing the local talent pool through education and training; attracting international talent; and preventing the outward migration of skilled professionals. Strategies to develop local talent centre on scholarships and fellowships, expanded academic career pathways, and academia–industry collaborations that supply research centres with researchers while giving them industry-relevant skills. Some universities also operate seed funds for academic staff pursuing startup ventures. Qatar implements comparable schemes, with the total number of scholarship programmes growing by 50% between 2012 and 2020.

Qatar has invested heavily in attracting talent, but retention lags

Qatar has expanded research funding and infrastructure, with QSTP and Education City as landmark developments, and introduced incentives such as the Alchemist Doha fund, the Technology Development Grant, and the Mustaqel Residency Visa covering 13 priority areas. Yet retention remains weak: many postdoctoral contracts expire shortly after the associated fellowship ends, prompting the premature exit of researchers and risking a net loss of locally trained expertise.

Retaining local talent is the hardest challenge

Fewer policies explicitly target retention than development or attraction, since much depends on employers offering competitive compensation and career progression. Despite reforms, including becoming the first GCC country to discontinue the Kafala system in 2020, international professionals still face precarious employment. Broader ecosystem improvements – stronger infrastructure and enhanced research opportunities – may indirectly support retention, but coordinated, employer-facing measures remain underdeveloped relative to the scale of the challenge.

Recommendations

Strengthen industry–academia crossover

Qatar may wish to consider programmes giving local postgraduate researchers greater industry exposure, drawing on models such as Spain's Ramón y Cajal and Juan de la Cierva schemes.

Extend entrepreneurial support to academia

There may be value in exploring university-based incubators that offer seed funding for feasible startup projects from within academia, alongside embedding entrepreneurship education within relevant university curricula.

Supporting researcher retention

Aligning visa durations more closely with realistic career timelines and improving post-fellowship continuity could help reduce the premature exit of researchers Qatar has invested in training.

items.body:
The Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) has five unique ionizing radiation sources. All sources are maintained and operated by the Survivable Electronics Technology group (AFRL/RJSV) at Kirtland AFB, NM. These sources allow partnering researchers from industry, government labs, and universities to study a wide spectrum of total ionizing dose and prompt dose effects. The Survivable Electronics Technology group primarily uses these sources to determine the effects of radiation on advanced microelectronics, photonics, sensors, and micro-electromechanical systems needed for Air Force, Space Force, Department of Defense, and government space and missile systems .

Services Provided

Dosimetry; both CaF 2 and Ion Chambers

Fabricate test board and boxes for devices under test

Machine Shop access

Supporting Equipment

Parametric Analyzers

B1500 w/ Switching Matrix

Keithley 4200

HP4142

Mixed Signal Tester

Operational Amplifiers

Analog-to-Digital Converters

Digital-to-Analog Converters

Memories

Oscilloscopes

Logic Analyzers

Clean-room

Cyrogenic Dewars

Annealing Ovens

Gamma Radiation Sources

Co-60

The Cobalt-60 source can deliver a maximum total ionizing dose of ~20 krad (Si)/min to a minimum of <1 rad (Si)/min (which falls within ASTM 1019 specs of 300 to 50 rad(Si)/sec). Slightly higher dose rates may be attained if researchers are willing to accept that the source will appear as a line source opposed to a point source. This source produces two energy peaks at 1.17 and 1.33 MeV. The irradiator is a 360-degree panoramic irradiator, facility area is 1,500 ft 2 which provides the researcher the benefit of a large range of variable dose rates with plenty of area to conduct experiments. Evaluation of subsystems is possible in this cell. The large area of the facility minimizes the possibility of dose enhancement due to scatter. The high energy photons give a uniform dose deposition throughout the sample of interest. AFRL Co-60 facility provides the capability of performing in-situ experiments whereby measurements on components are taken during gamma irradiation through the use of 120 ft of BNC cables and CAT-5 cables that would allow the experimenters to control computer-controlled instrumentation from the control room to the irradiation test cell.

Total Dose Simulator

1.17 & 1.33 MeV Gammas

<.001 to 20 krad(Si)/min

1500 ft 2 of Test Cell

360-degree panoramic irradiator

Cesium

The Cesium 137 low dose rate source will deliver a maximum of 40 rad(Si)/hr or a minimum of 0.3 rad(Si)/hr. This source produces gamma rays with a single energy peak at 662 keV. The Cs-137 source is capable of housing experiments which can fit in 1 ft 3 of volume. Due to the small exposure volume, a Pb/Al box is required for all experiments performed in this source to eliminate a dose enhancement effect. Will provide a Pb/Al box for experiments which meets ASTM standards if users do not have one. This source is capable of providing in-situ experimentation.

Low Total Dose Simulator

662 keV Gammas

0.005 to 0.667 rad(Si)/min

2.25 ft 2 Test Cell

X-Ray Radiation Sources

ARACOR X-Ray

The ARACOR X-ray test system is used to investigate total ionizing dose effects on individual microelectronic devices. This system produces X-rays with energies that have a max range of 60 keV with peak energies at 10 keV and dose rates ranging from 0.1 to 30 krad (SiO 2 )/min. The system is capable to accommodating an 8” wafer for X-ray characterization of fabricated die or packaged devices with lids removed. Capable of utilizing a probe card to probe and bias up to 48 contacts concurrently.

10 to 60 keV spectrum, peak 10 keV

0.1 to 30 krad (SiO 2 )/min

Low Energy X-Ray (LEXR)

The Low Energy X-ray source is a Comet MXR-160/22 constant potential X-ray system which produces X-rays with energies that have a max range of 10 keV to 160 keV and peaks at 10 keV and 60 keV depending on the applied voltage. This source can produce a total ionizing dose rate of 360 krad (SiO 2 )/min. Exposure area is a 1.84 cm diameter at 10 cm from the X-ray tube. The distance from the tube can be varied up to 1 m to control dose rate. The X-ray tube current is variable in order to control dose rate, and the total energy deposited per unit area. This source is capable of providing in-situ experimentation.

High Total Dose Simulator

10 to 160 keV spectrum, peaks 10 and 60 keV(adjustable)

360 krad(SiO 2 )/min (max)

30 ft 2 Test Cell

Flash X-Ray (FXR)

The Flash X-ray source is a Febetron 705 machine which produces prompt dose exposures simulating nuclear weapons environments. This facility is capable of producing a 20 nanosecond pulse X-ray. The average 2.1 MeV of the X-rays produced in this facility provides a dose rate output from between 1x10 7 to 2x10 11 rad (Si)/sec. A 70 ft 2 . screen room is available for housing experiments in order to minimize the effects of EMP produced by the Febetron 705. To obtain higher dose rates, experiments may be performed in open air directly in front of the Febetron 705.

items.title: Examining the Evolution of Veteran Labor Market Outcomes
items.author: Jeffrey B. Wenger
items.summary: In this report, the authors examine how military service connects to earnings in the civilian labor market by tracking veterans’ and non-veterans’ labor market outcomes eight years after entering the civilian workforce.
items.body:
In this report, the authors examine how military service connects to earnings in the civilian labor market by tracking veterans’ and non-veterans’ labor market outcomes eight years after entering the civilian workforce. The authors linked data from two major U.S. Census Bureau datasets to compare veterans’ and non-veterans’ earnings outcomes over time while accounting for observable differences.

Examining the Evolution of Veteran Labor Market Outcomes

Lisa Abraham , Christine Mulhern , Isaac M. Opper , Prateek Puri , Elizabeth Roth , Jeffrey B. Wenger

Research Published Sep 15, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

The transition from military service to civilian employment can be difficult for veterans: They must translate military skills into civilian job terms, decide whether to pursue additional education, and present their backgrounds to employers who may not understand how military experience maps onto civilian roles. These early transition challenges may have lasting implications for veterans’ earnings trajectories. Yet despite these hurdles, relatively little research examines how veterans fare over the long term in the civilian labor force after leaving the military.

In this report, the authors examine how military service connects to earnings in the civilian labor market by tracking veterans’ and non-veterans’ labor market outcomes eight years after entering the civilian workforce. The authors linked data from the Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics program—the largest longitudinal panel of U.S. worker employment—to data from the American Community Survey to follow workers’ earnings from 2005 to 2019.

The resulting dataset allows the authors to account for factors that are usually unavailable in administrative data, such as characteristics of a worker’s initial occupation. The authors used these data to compare veterans’ and non-veterans’ earnings outcomes over time while accounting for observable differences.

Key Takeaways

In this sample, veterans’ earnings grew faster than comparable non-veterans’ over the eight years after labor market entry.

Although veterans started with slightly lower earnings, their earnings grew about 10 percentage points more than non-veterans’ over that period.

This earnings growth advantage was present across demographic groups, including male, female, Black, Asian, Hispanic, and White veterans.

More research—especially datasets that link veterans’ military service histories to comprehensive civilian employment records, including federal employment—is needed to comprehensively understand veterans’ military-to-civilian labor market transition.

items.title: A U.S. Strategy to Secure Geopolitical Advantage on an Uncertain Path to Superintelligence
items.author: Tobias Sytsma
items.summary: Frontier artificial intelligence continues to advance, and many experts contend that superintelligence is possible. The authors recommend a Freedom of Action strategy to secure geopolitical advantage and ensure humanity’s survival with agency.
items.body:
Maintaining Freedom of Action

Joel B. Predd , Benjamin Boudreaux , Matt Chessen , Beba Cibralic , Edward Geist , Kamaria Horton , Amanda Kerrigan , William Marcellino , Shanshan Mei , Jared Mondschein , et al.

Expert Insights Published Sep 15, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Frontier artificial intelligence (AI) continues to advance, and an increasing number of experts contend that the creation of superintelligence is possible. Although progress might slow or even halt, the transformative potential of superintelligence demands proactive strategy-making. The stakes are high, not only for geopolitics, but for humanity’s survival and agency. What, then, should U.S. strategy be? Should the United States pursue AI supremacy by monopolizing the frontier? Co-develop superintelligence with rivals? Deter its advance? Pause and freeze its development? And in a competitive environment, how will other powers and geopolitical rivals respond to the choices they face?

In this paper, the authors argue that seven archetypal strategies dominate the debate, that current evidence cannot resolve five pivotal uncertainties about the most feasible and sensible strategy, and that committing prematurely to any one of them, or deferring commitment too long, forecloses options. They therefore recommend a Freedom of Action strategy to build and preserve the ability to secure geopolitical advantage and ensure humanity’s survival with agency through the transition to superintelligence.

items.summary: The author examines the U.S. Air Force’s challenges and options as it faces emerging aerial threats, especially small drones. The analysis highlights the need for new capabilities, integration, and clear authority to secure future air base defense.
items.body:
Sean M. Zeigler

Expert Insights Published Sep 15, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

U.S. air base defense is at an inflection point: It faces new challenges as legacy Army–Air Force arrangements fail to address emerging aerial threats, especially small drones. These inexpensive, adaptable systems expose vulnerabilities in installations reliant on overstretched Army defenses. In this paper, the author examines the evolving challenge of defending U.S. Air Force installations against a rapidly expanding spectrum of aerial threats, with a focus on small unmanned aerial systems.

Technological developments and recent organizational changes, including counter–small unmanned aerial system responsibility shifts and the Golden Dome and Joint Interagency Task Force 401 initiatives, give the Air Force an opportunity to redefine its air base defense role. Options include developing organic counter-drone and short-range defenses and integrating with joint sensing networks.

The analysis underscores the interplay of threat evolution, interservice responsibilities, and policy considerations that shape how the U.S. military protects its critical airpower assets. To secure its bases, the Air Force must rethink boundaries, set priorities, and clearly define needed capabilities and authorities to shape future air base defense.

items.title: AFRL demonstrates modular multimode propulsion system for sustained space maneuver
items.author: Patrick Londergan
